notes.title: HTTP Methods & Their Contracts

headings.text: When would you use PUT to create a resource instead of POST?
You're designing an update endpoint for a 40-field user profile. PUT or PATCH?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Method reference — MDN: HTTP request methods

  • Normative semantics — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, §9 Methods

  • Status codes methods return — MDN: HTTP response status codes

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
PUT vs PATCH in one line? PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH applies a partial change document.
Who owns the ID: PUT or POST creation? PUT — the client picks the URI. POST — the server assigns it.
What must a 405 response carry? An Allow header listing the methods that URI does support.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A method is a contract about intent, and the server is expected to honour it. GET reads, POST submits something for processing, PUT replaces a resource at a URI the client already knows, PATCH applies a partial change, DELETE removes. HEAD is GET without a body, so it is the cheap way to check existence or size. OPTIONS reports what a URI supports and is what the browser fires as a CORS preflight. The properties those contracts imply — safe, idempotent, cacheable — are where the operational consequences actually live. (→ Item 58)

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

When would you use PUT to create a resource instead of POST?

The deciding question is who owns the identifier. POST /orders means "here is a thing, you name it" — the server assigns ord_9f2c and returns 201 with a Location header. PUT /orders/9f2c-4a1e means "make the resource at this URI look like this body", which only works if the client can generate an identifier the server will accept, normally a UUID. Choose PUT when the client can own identity, because you get retry safety for free: a duplicate PUT overwrites with the same content instead of creating a second order.

Choose POST when the ID must be server-generated — a sequential invoice number, an ID issued by a downstream system, or anything where the client must not influence the key space. The cost is that POST creation is not retryable on its own, so you have to add idempotency keys to get back what PUT gave you by contract. (→ Item 67) HEAD and OPTIONS sit outside this axis entirely: HEAD returns GET's headers with no body, so Content-Length or ETag answer existence and size questions without transferring the payload, and OPTIONS advertises capability.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

You're designing an update endpoint for a 40-field user profile. PUT or PATCH?

📍 Seen in the wild: surfaces as "the mobile client keeps wiping fields it doesn't know about".

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name the flip condition instead of reciting both definitions.

I default to PUT, because full replacement is idempotent by construction and trivially retryable, and because it makes lost-field bugs loud rather than silent. The failure mode PUT creates is real though: any client that fetches, edits two fields and PUTs back will erase every field added to the schema after that client shipped. That is the classic mobile-app regression — an old binary round-trips a resource and quietly deletes the fields it never learned about.

The flip condition is payload size or field ownership. Flip to PATCH when the resource is large enough that a full round trip is wasteful, or when different clients legitimately own different subsets of the fields and must not overwrite each other's. Then use JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) with Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json, keep the document declarative so it stays idempotent, and pair it with If-Match and an ETag so concurrent partial updates cannot clobber each other. (→ Item 61)

4. Quick Comparison Table

Method Semantics Request body Success code Notes
GET Retrieve a representation ❌ (ignored) 200, 206 Cacheable by default; never give it side effects
HEAD GET's headers, no body ❌ 200 Existence, size, ETag checks for free
POST Submit for processing ✅ 201 + Location, 200, 202 Server owns the new ID
PUT Replace resource at this URI ✅ (full) 200, 201, 204 Client owns the ID; idempotent
PATCH Apply a partial change ✅ (patch doc) 200, 204 Idempotency depends on the document
DELETE Remove the resource ❌ usually 204, 200, 202 404 on repeat is still idempotent
OPTIONS Report capabilities ❌ 204, 200 + Allow Also the CORS preflight

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No math — the mechanism is a workflow. This is the dispatch a well-behaved server runs before any handler code executes.

The branch worth checking in your own framework is the 405 arm: RFC 9110 §15.5.6 makes Allow mandatory on a 405, and most hand-rolled routers omit it. Returning 404 instead of 405 for a wrong method is the other common shortcut — it hides routing bugs and breaks clients that probe capability.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't put state changes behind GET. Crawlers, link-preview bots and browser prefetchers fire GETs unprompted; a GET /items/5/delete route gets exercised by a search engine eventually. The detection signal is destructive actions appearing in access logs with a bot user agent.

Don't use PUT when the server must own the identifier. Sequential invoice numbers, downstream-issued account IDs and anything with a meaningful key space belong to POST plus a Location header. Letting clients choose keys there is a collision and enumeration problem.

Don't reach for PATCH before you have a concurrency story. Partial updates from multiple clients without If-Match produce lost updates that no log line records — the write succeeds, the earlier field value just disappears. (→ Item 61)

Don't invent methods. Proxies, CDNs and corporate middleboxes drop or mishandle anything outside the standard set, and the failure appears only on some networks. Model the verb in the URI or the body instead.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "PUT means update and POST means create."

✅ Reality: Both can create. PUT creates when the client already knows the target URI, and returns 201 the first time and 200 or 204 afterwards. POST creates when the server assigns the URI. The real axis is identifier ownership, not create-versus-update — and it's the axis that decides whether a retry is safe.

❌ Misconception: "OPTIONS is just a CORS thing browsers do."

✅ Reality: OPTIONS is a general capability-discovery method in RFC 9110 that returns Allow for a URI; the CORS preflight is one application of it that adds Access-Control-* headers. Servers that special-case only the CORS shape break the plain OPTIONS * case and hand back a useless empty 200 to any client probing what a resource supports.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • HTTP as a protocol (Item 44) — the request line these methods occupy.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — the properties each method carries. Read immediately after this.

  • Choosing the right status code (Item 60) — the response half of the contract, including 405 and 412.

  • Headers that matter (Item 61) — Allow, If-Match and the negotiation headers methods depend on.

  • Idempotency keys (Item 67) — what POST needs to become as retryable as PUT.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Method properties (normative) — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, §9.2 Common Method Properties

  • Idempotency — MDN Glossary: Idempotent

  • Safety — MDN Glossary: Safe (HTTP Methods)

  • Method reference — MDN: HTTP request methods

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Define all three in one line. Safe = no state change · Idempotent = repeating changes nothing further · Cacheable = a response may be stored and reused.
Which methods are idempotent but not safe? PUT and DELETE. They change state, but repeating adds nothing.
Is PATCH idempotent? No, not by default. {"$inc": {"qty": 1}} applied twice adds two.
Does idempotent mean identical response? No. DELETE twice gives 204 then 404 — the effect is idempotent, the response isn't.
Why does this property matter operationally? It is the single thing that decides whether a proxy, client or retry loop may safely resend.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Day before interview — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three independent properties, and people constantly collapse them. Safe means the request isn't intended to change state, so a crawler can fire it freely. Idempotent means sending it twice leaves the system in the same place as sending it once — which is what actually licenses a retry. Cacheable means a response may be stored and served to a later request. GET is all three; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST and PATCH are none of them. The reason to be precise is that every retry, every proxy, and every load balancer in your path is making decisions based on which bucket your method falls into.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through which methods have which properties, and why PATCH is the awkward one.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the properties are independent, rather than one spectrum.

GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are safe, and everything safe is automatically idempotent. PUT and DELETE are idempotent without being safe: PUT replaces a resource with the body you supplied, so five PUTs leave the state one would, and DELETE finds nothing left to remove on the second call. POST is neither — its contract is "submit this to be processed", with no promise about what processing means. Cacheability is the odd one out: GET and HEAD by default, POST only with explicit freshness info, which almost nothing implements.

PATCH is awkward because idempotency depends on the patch document, not the method. A merge patch setting {"status": "shipped"} is idempotent; a patch containing an increment or an array append is not. So the spec cannot declare PATCH idempotent and a proxy cannot assume it — if you want retryable PATCH you make it so yourself, by keeping the document declarative or attaching an If-Match precondition.

Worth stating explicitly: these describe the intended effect, not the response. Deleting twice returns 204 then 404 — different responses, identical resulting state, fully idempotent.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A POST /orders timed out. The client doesn't know if the order was created. What are your options?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard entry point into an idempotency-key discussion; often phrased as "how do you make a payment API safe".

🎯 Really testing: whether you reach for a protocol-level fix or start inventing application heuristics.

The honest first observation is that the client cannot know, and no retry logic changes that — a timeout is ambiguous by construction: the request may have been lost outbound, processed and lost inbound, or still be running. So the question is which of three designs you adopt.

Make it idempotent by design: have the client PUT to a client-chosen identifier, PUT /orders/{uuid}. Retrying is then free by contract. The cost is pushing ID generation to the client — fine for orders, awkward when the server owns a meaningful sequence. Or use idempotency keys: keep POST, require an Idempotency-Key the server stores alongside the first response and replays on any repeat. That preserves server-side IDs, at the cost of a store with a TTL and a uniqueness constraint you must get right under concurrency. (→ Item 67)

The third option is client-side reconciliation — GET the order list by client reference before retrying. I'd reject it as a primary design: racy, an extra unhappy-path round trip, and it assumes the read path is consistent with the write path. It's the answer only for a legacy server I can't change.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Your load balancer is configured to retry failed requests. What breaks, and at what scale does it start hurting?

📍 Seen in the wild: recurring incident; often surfaces as "we got duplicate charges" or "one bad deploy took down the whole tier".

Two distinct failures at different scales. The correctness failure arrives immediately: if the proxy retries non-idempotent methods, a POST /payments that succeeded but lost its response gets replayed and the customer is charged twice. One dropped response is enough — load is irrelevant. The fix is to scope retries to idempotent methods, or to requests carrying an idempotency key.

The availability failure arrives under load and is worse, because retries multiply per layer. Browser, gateway and service client each retrying three times turns one user request into twenty-seven backend requests worst case. That amplification is harmless while the backend is healthy and catastrophic exactly when it isn't — the moment latency rises, every layer starts retrying at once and piles load onto an already-struggling tier. It's a positive feedback loop: the system's response to overload is more load.

The fixes are structural, not parametric. Retry at exactly one layer. Use a retry budget capping retries at 10–20% of successful requests, which bounds amplification to a constant instead of a power. Add jitter so retries don't synchronise, and a circuit breaker so retrying stops when a dependency is clearly down. The forming signal is attempted-to-unique request ratio per hop: near 1.0 steady-state, past ~1.2 means the retry policy is now part of the problem. (→ Item 68)

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the write path for an API that triggers expensive, non-reversible side effects — a payment, or an LLM generation billed per token.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat exactly-once as achievable, and whether you can name where the deduplication state actually lives.

I'd start by rejecting exactly-once delivery as a goal — it isn't achievable over an unreliable network. What is achievable is at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing, which produces exactly-once effects. I'm not preventing duplicate arrivals, I'm making them harmless. The client generates a UUID per logical operation as Idempotency-Key; the server's first action, before any side effect, is an atomic insert of that key under a uniqueness constraint.

Atomicity is the part that's easy to get wrong. A naive "check then process" races: two concurrent retries both check, both find nothing, both charge. The insert must be the concurrency primitive — insert in a processing state and let the uniqueness constraint reject the loser, which then polls for the winner's result or returns 409 so the client retries into the replayed response. The record stores the response body and status plus a fingerprint of the request, so the same key with a different body is rejected rather than silently replaying the wrong answer. TTL must exceed the client's total retry window — 24 hours is the common choice.

For the LLM case I'd add one thing payments don't need: a replay must return the stored completion rather than regenerating, since generation is the expensive part. That makes the record large, so I'd keep the body in object storage behind a pointer. The failure I'd instrument first is silent: rising key collisions with mismatched request fingerprints means clients are reusing keys across different operations, which will eventually hand one customer another's response.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Method Safe Idempotent Cacheable Typical use
GET ✅ ✅ ✅ Read a resource
HEAD ✅ ✅ ✅ Metadata only, no body
OPTIONS ✅ ✅ ❌ Capability discovery, CORS preflight
PUT ❌ ✅ ❌ Replace a resource at a known URI
DELETE ❌ ✅ ❌ Remove a resource
POST ❌ ❌ Only with explicit freshness Submit for processing
PATCH ❌ Depends on the patch document ❌ Partial modification

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Reading the meter, setting the dial, nudging the dial.

You read the meter on the wall — do it ten times, nothing about the room changes. You set the thermostat dial to 20° — the room changes, but setting it to 20 again five times leaves it at exactly 20. You nudge the dial up one degree — do that five times and you're at 25, not 21.

Story beat Mechanism
Reading the meter GET — safe, and therefore idempotent
Setting the dial to an absolute value PUT — not safe, but idempotent
Nudging by a relative amount PATCH with an increment — neither
The room's final temperature Server state, which is what the properties describe
The number you read off after The response, which may differ even when the effect doesn't

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No math — the mechanism is a decision procedure that every retrying component runs, explicitly or by accident.

The three properties are independent, not a hierarchy — with one implication running one way only:

                 SAFE ──────────► implies ──────────► IDEMPOTENT
            (no state change)                    (repeat = same state)
                   │                                     │
                   ▼                                     ▼
              GET, HEAD                            + PUT, DELETE
              OPTIONS, TRACE

  CACHEABLE is orthogonal: GET/HEAD by default; POST only with explicit
  freshness info; PUT/DELETE never (they are not responses you may reuse).

  The one-way arrow matters: every safe method is idempotent,
  but plenty of idempotent methods are not safe.

7. Why It Matters in Production

Every retry decision in your stack silently depends on this. Your HTTP client, your load balancer and your service mesh each have a default retry policy deciding, from the method, whether resending is safe — and when one is wrong you get duplicate writes that present as data corruption rather than as a networking bug, which is why they take so long to diagnose.

It also decides what your CDN and reverse proxy do without asking. A GET response may be stored and served to another user; getting Cache-Control and Vary wrong on a personalised GET is how one customer sees another's data. (→ Item 62)

8. Code / Pseudocode Example

The same operation designed three ways. This is the example traced in Section 9.

import uuid, httpx

order = {"sku": "ABC-123", "qty": 2}

# (a) NOT retryable — server generates the ID, so a replay creates a second order.
r = httpx.post("https://api.example.com/orders", json=order)

# (b) Idempotent BY DESIGN — client owns the identifier, so PUT's contract covers us.
#     Retrying is free: the second PUT overwrites with identical content.
order_id = uuid.uuid4()
r = httpx.put(f"https://api.example.com/orders/{order_id}", json=order)

# (c) Idempotent BY KEY — keep POST and server-generated IDs, add a dedup token.
#     The key must be generated ONCE per logical operation and reused across
#     every retry of that operation — regenerating it defeats the whole mechanism.
key = str(uuid.uuid4())
for attempt in range(3):
    r = httpx.post("https://api.example.com/orders", json=order,
                   headers={"Idempotency-Key": key})   # same key every attempt
    if r.status_code < 500:
        break

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Same three designs. In each, the request reaches the server, the order is created, and the response is lost on the way back — so the client times out and retries once.

📥 Client sends order {sku: ABC-123, qty: 2}. Server succeeds. Response lost.
    │
    ├── (a) POST /orders, no key ──────────────────────────┐
    │      🔁 retry → server has no way to recognise it
    │      🗄️  orders table: ord_001, ord_002
    │      ❌ TWO ORDERS. Customer charged twice.
    │
    ├── (b) PUT /orders/9f2c-...  (client UUID) ───────────┐
    │      🔁 retry → same URI, same body
    │      🗄️  orders table: 9f2c-... (overwritten, identical)
    │      ✅ ONE ORDER. Idempotent by protocol contract.
    │
    └── (c) POST /orders + Idempotency-Key: 7a1e-... ──────┐
           🔁 retry → server finds key 7a1e-… already committed
           🗄️  orders table: ord_001 · idem table: 7a1e-… → ord_001
           ✅ ONE ORDER, and the stored 201 response is replayed

  1. Case (a) fails because the server has no identity to deduplicate on. Body equality is no substitute — two distinct orders for the same SKU and quantity are legitimate, so the server cannot tell a retry from a real second order.

  2. Case (b) works because the identifier moved to the client. PUT's contract is "make the resource at this URI look like this body", idempotent by definition. The trade is losing server-side ID assignment, which matters if IDs must be sequential or issued downstream.

  3. Case (c) works because the key supplies identity without moving ID generation. Note the retry sends the same key — a client regenerating it per attempt has an ordinary non-idempotent POST wearing a header. This is the most common implementation bug in the pattern.

  4. All three rest on one fact: a timeout is ambiguous, so the design must make the ambiguity harmless rather than resolve it.

10. When TO Use This

Reach for it whenever you configure retries anywhere — client library, proxy, mesh, job runner. The method's properties are the input to that decision, and the default is usually wrong for POST.

Use it when designing an API surface: PUT with a client-supplied ID over POST is a deliberate purchase of retry safety, worth making consciously.

Use it when reviewing a caching layer — mismatches here produce cross-user data leaks, not mere staleness.

Use it when side effects are expensive or irreversible — payments, emails, LLM generation, provisioning — where a duplicate is a business incident rather than a nuisance.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't treat "idempotent by spec" as "idempotent in your implementation". DELETE is idempotent by contract, but a handler that decrements a counter or fires a webhook on every call has broken it. The spec constrains what clients may assume — and clients will retry on that assumption.

Don't rely on idempotency to fix ordering. It makes a duplicate harmless; it does nothing about two different updates arriving out of order. That needs versioning and preconditions — If-Match with an ETag. (→ Item 61)

Don't assume PATCH is retry-safe because it was last year. Idempotency depends on the patch document, so a payload change can silently make a previously-safe retry path unsafe.

Don't use idempotency keys where a natural key exists. An invoice number or webhook delivery ID with a uniqueness constraint is simpler and more durable than a parallel key store with a TTL.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Idempotent means you get the same response every time."

✅ Reality: It means the server state ends up the same. DELETE /orders/5 returns 204 the first time and 404 the second — different responses, identical resulting state, and that is fully idempotent. Conflating the two leads people to call correct implementations broken, and to "fix" them by returning 204 for deletes of things that never existed.

❌ Misconception: "GET is safe, so it can't cause any side effects."

✅ Reality: Safe expresses intent, not enforcement. Servers routinely log, increment counters and refresh sessions on GET. What safety promises is that the client isn't requesting a state change — which is why crawlers, prefetchers and link-preview bots fire GETs freely. Putting a destructive action behind a GET is how sites get wiped by a crawler.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning):

❌ I treated the three properties as a single scale of "how dangerous is this method", with GET at one end and POST at the other.

✅ They're independent axes answering different questions: safe answers "may I send this at all?", idempotent answers "may I send it again?", cacheable answers "may I store the reply?". A method can be idempotent and not cacheable (PUT). Once I separated them, retry and caching questions stopped blurring together — they were never the same question.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Saying "POST is not idempotent" without saying what to do about it. The property is the setup; the mechanism is the answer — client-supplied IDs with PUT, or idempotency keys.

Claiming exactly-once delivery. Not achievable over an unreliable network. The senior phrasing is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, yielding exactly-once effects. Interviewers listen for this correction specifically.

Forgetting these are contracts clients rely on, not descriptions. You keep DELETE idempotent because proxies and client libraries retry it without asking you.

Missing the retry-amplification angle. Idempotency makes a retry correct, not safe under load. Solving duplicates without mentioning retry budgets or circuit breakers answers half the question. (→ Item 68)

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Safe methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE All are also idempotent RFC 9110 §9.2.1
Idempotent methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE POST and PATCH excluded RFC 9110 §9.2.2
Cacheable by default GET, HEAD POST only with explicit freshness info RFC 9110 §9.2.3
Stripe idempotency key retention 24 hours Must exceed the client's full retry window Stripe API docs
Retry amplification, 3 layers × 3 attempts 27× worst case Why retries belong at exactly one layer Derived (3³)
Typical retry budget cap 10–20% of successful requests Bounds amplification to a constant Common practice — verify against your mesh's default

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Idempotency keys add a store write on the critical path before any work begins — typically a single-digit ms same-DC round trip, paid on every request to save the rare duplicate.
💰 Cost The dedup store is pure overhead in the happy path. For expensive operations (payments, LLM generation) it pays for itself the first time it prevents one duplicate.
🎯 Quality Correct properties are what make retries safe, which is what turns transient failures into invisible ones. This is the largest single lever on user-visible error rate.
📈 Scale The dedup store must handle full write QPS and needs a TTL sweep. At scale it becomes a real dependency with its own availability budget — and a hard one, since it sits in front of the write path.
🔧 Ops Complexity Client-supplied IDs (PUT) are nearly free operationally. Idempotency keys add a store, a TTL policy, a concurrency race to get right, and a request-fingerprint mismatch case to handle.

16. Real World Usage

Stripe accepts Idempotency-Key on POST requests and retains results for 24 hours — the de facto convention most payment and billing APIs have copied.

S3's PUT object is idempotent by design: the client supplies the key, so re-uploading identical content converges. This is why S3 uploads are trivially retryable and POST-based upload APIs usually aren't.

Kubernetes' declarative apply generalises the pattern past HTTP — you PUT desired state rather than POSTing a change, so a controller reconciling repeatedly is safe by construction.

Envoy and gRPC retry policies expose retry budgets as first-class config precisely because the Tier 3 amplification problem is well known.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • HTTP methods & their contracts (Item 57) — the methods this note classifies.

  • HTTP as a protocol (Item 44) — statelessness is why these properties have to be declared rather than inferred.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • Idempotency keys (Item 67) — the mechanism that gives POST what PUT gets for free. Read this next.

  • Timeouts, retries & backoff (Item 68) — the client-side contract these properties license.

  • Choosing the right status code (Item 60) — 409 and 412 are the codes idempotency and precondition failures produce.

  • HTTP caching (Item 62) — the cacheability axis in operational detail.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Client-generated IDs with PUT — choose it when the client can own identity; simplest possible retry safety, no dedup store.

  • Natural unique keys with a DB constraint — choose it when the operation already has real-world identity (invoice number, delivery ID).

  • At-most-once with reconciliation — choose it only when you cannot change the server; racy and adds an unhappy-path round trip.

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • ETags and If-Match (Item 61) — preconditions handle ordering, which idempotency does not.

  • Rate limiting (Item 69) — 429 is a retryable failure, so its interaction with the retry policy matters.

  • L4 vs L7 load balancing (Item 4) — the proxy's retry configuration is exactly this decision, made in config.

19. System Design Application

"Skipped — this is a protocol property rather than a system; the architect-level treatment is carried by the Section 3 Tier 4 follow-up, and the distinct system-level design (dedup store, TTL, concurrency, capacity) belongs to Item 67, where it is the whole topic rather than a corollary."

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The full registry — MDN: HTTP response status codes

  • Normative definitions — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, §15 Status Codes

  • Retry signalling — MDN: Retry-After

  • Preconditions and 304/412 — MDN: ETag

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
302 vs 307 — the one real difference? 307 forbids rewriting POST to GET. 302 clients rewrite it.
502 vs 503 vs 504? Reached upstream, got garbage · nowhere to send it · upstream too slow.
Which code MUST carry Allow? 405 Method Not Allowed — list the methods that are permitted.
404 vs 410? 410 means deliberately and permanently gone. 404 promises nothing.
401 vs 403? 401 = who are you, retry with credentials. 403 = known, still refused.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Day before interview — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

The class is the contract; the code is the detail. 2xx says it worked, 3xx says look elsewhere, 4xx says the client must change something before retrying, 5xx says the server failed and the same request might work later. That split is what every retry loop, proxy and dashboard keys off. The codes worth precision are the pairs people collapse: 401 versus 403, 404 versus 410, 302 versus 307, and the 502/503/504 triad that names which hop broke.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through the classes, and the codes inside them that people actually get wrong.

🎯 Really testing: whether you use the codes as a vocabulary or just reach for 200 and 500.

In 2xx the distinctions carry data. 201 Created MUST carry Location pointing at the thing you made, or the client guesses the URI. 202 Accepted means "I took it, I have not done it", so the body owes the caller a status or polling URL; a 202 with an empty body is a dead end. 204 No Content is success with deliberately nothing to send — not the same as 200 with an empty object.

In 4xx the confusions are the interview. 401 means unauthenticated and pairs with WWW-Authenticate; 403 means the server knows who you are and still refuses, so re-authenticating is pointless. 404 says nothing about whether the resource ever existed; 410 Gone asserts deliberate permanent removal, which lets crawlers and caches drop the link. 405 MUST include Allow. 415 rejects the media type, 422 accepts the syntax and rejects the meaning, 409 says the request fights current state, and 412 says your If-Match no longer holds. (→ Item 61)

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Which redirect do you pick, and why do 307 and 308 exist at all?

📍 Seen in the wild: an HTTPS upgrade or a path rename that silently turns every POST into a GET and drops the body.

Method preservation is the load-bearing point. 301 and 302 were implemented so widely, and so early, that clients rewrite a POST into a GET when following them and drop the body; the spec documented that reality rather than fighting it. 307 and 308 exist purely to forbid the rewrite: same method, same body, new URI.

So the choice is a two-by-two. Permanent and method-preserving is 308, permanent and don't-care is 301; temporary and method-preserving is 307, temporary and don't-care is 302. For an API that accepts POST, 307/308 are the only safe answers — a 301 on POST /v1/charges becomes GET /v1/charges with no body, and the client sees a bewildering 405.

303 See Other is the deliberate opposite: switch to GET on purpose. That is the POST/redirect/GET pattern, which stops a browser refresh resubmitting a form. 304 Not Modified is not a redirect at all — it is a validator response meaning "your stored copy is still good". (→ Item 62)

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Your dashboard shows a spike of 502s, 503s and 504s. Triage them.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know these are three different failures emitted by different components, not three flavours of "backend sad".

📍 Seen in the wild: every load-balancer incident review; the first question is always which of the three dominates.

All three are emitted by the intermediary — load balancer, ingress or mesh sidecar — not by your application. Say that first: it tells you the app logs may be empty.

502 Bad Gateway: the proxy reached an upstream and got something unusable — a reset mid-response, a malformed reply, a protocol mismatch. Check pods killed mid-request (OOM, liveness restarts), and idle-timeout mismatch where the upstream closes keep-alive connections before the proxy expects.

503 Service Unavailable: the proxy had nowhere to send it. No healthy backend, or an admission-control or concurrency limit rejected it before dispatch. Nothing was attempted, so check health-check config and pool membership first, then queue limits. A 503 should carry Retry-After.

504 Gateway Timeout: an upstream accepted it and did not finish in time. The work may still be running — this is the ambiguous one for writes. Check upstream latency percentiles and the proxy's own timeout budget, which is often shorter than the app's. (→ Item 68)

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the error contract for a public API.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat errors as an API surface with a compatibility guarantee, or as strings.

One body shape for every error on every endpoint, in the RFC 9457 problem-detail style: a stable machine-readable code, a human title, the numeric status, a detail, and a request ID the caller can quote in a ticket. Clients branch on the code, never the prose — so the prose stays free to change and the code becomes a versioned part of the contract.

Class assignment follows one rule: 4xx means retrying this exact request fails again, 5xx means it might succeed. That rule is what makes the contract usable by a generic retry layer. So a validation failure is 422 even when it crashed a parser, and an overloaded dependency is 503 with Retry-After rather than 500 — because 500 says nothing about whether to wait.

The 4xx bodies are where you leak. Never confirm a resource the caller cannot access — 404 rather than 403 for another tenant's object, or you have built an enumeration oracle. Never echo internal identifiers, table names, upstream hostnames or stack traces; put those behind the request ID, in your logs.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Confusable pair The distinction Client should
401 vs 403 Unauthenticated vs authenticated-but-refused Re-auth vs give up
404 vs 410 Unknown vs deliberately, permanently gone Maybe retry vs purge the link
400 vs 422 Syntax unparseable vs semantics invalid Fix the encoding vs fix the fields
409 vs 412 Conflicts with current state vs your precondition failed Re-read and merge vs re-read the ETag
301/302 vs 308/307 Method may be rewritten vs MUST be preserved Watch for a dropped POST body
302 vs 303 Method left ambiguous vs deliberately switch to GET 303 is the POST/redirect/GET tool
502 vs 503 vs 504 Bad reply vs no backend vs too slow Retry all three, but debug differently
500 vs 501 We broke vs we never implemented this Retry vs never retry

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

The waiter comes back from the kitchen with three different bad answers.

You order the fish. The waiter walks to the kitchen and returns with a plate of something charred and unidentifiable — 502: he reached the kitchen, what came back was unusable. Another night he returns immediately: no chef on shift, kitchen door bolted — 503, nobody to hand the order to, come back in twenty minutes. A third night the chef takes the order and forty minutes later the waiter gives up and comes back empty-handed — 504, accepted but never finished, and your fish may still be cooking.

Story beat Mechanism
The waiter The proxy, LB or ingress — it emits all three, not the app
Charred unidentifiable plate 502 — upstream reached, reply malformed or connection reset
Kitchen bolted, no chef 503 — no healthy backend or admission limit rejected it
"Come back in twenty minutes" Retry-After on the 503
Chef took it, never returned 504 — upstream accepted, exceeded the proxy's timeout
Your fish may still be cooking Why 504 on a write is ambiguous and needs idempotency (→ Item 67)

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No math — the mechanism is a classification decision procedure the server runs in a fixed order, and the order is what makes the codes informative.

  CLASS   MEANING                      WHO EMITS IT          CLIENT'S DEFAULT MOVE
  ─────   ──────────────────────────   ───────────────────   ─────────────────────────
  1xx     Interim, keep going          origin                wait (100-continue, 101)
  2xx     It worked                    origin                done
  3xx     Look elsewhere               origin or edge        follow, watch the method
  4xx     YOU must change something    origin or edge        do NOT retry unchanged
  5xx     WE failed, may work later    origin OR any hop     retry with backoff+jitter

  The 4xx/5xx line is the retry boundary. Two codes deliberately cross it:
    429 - a 4xx you SHOULD retry, after Retry-After elapses
    408 - request timeout; the client may resend

The order in the flowchart is the contract. Authorisation is checked before existence so you never confirm a resource you would not serve; media type (415) is checked before field semantics (422) because you cannot judge fields you could not parse.

7. Why It Matters in Production

Status codes are the only part of an error every layer in the path agrees on. Your retry library, circuit breaker, CDN and alerting rules all branch on them without reading your body — so a handler returning 500 for a validation failure makes every one of those layers retry a request that can never succeed.

They are also your incident vocabulary. A single "5xx rate" panel is close to useless: it merges a code bug (500) with three infrastructure failures (502/503/504) that have different owners and different first checks. Separate series per code, split by emitting hop, is the difference between a five-minute triage and an hour of guessing.

8. Code / Pseudocode Example

A FastAPI submit endpoint whose only job is to pick the right code. This is the example traced in Section 9.

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response, HTTPException
app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/v1/transcripts", status_code=202)
def submit(req: Request, body: dict, response: Response):
    # 415 BEFORE 422: you cannot judge fields you could not parse.
    if req.headers.get("content-type") != "application/json":
        raise HTTPException(415, "send application/json")
    # 422, not 400: the syntax parsed fine, the MEANING is wrong.
    if body.get("duration_s", 0) > 7200:
        raise HTTPException(422, "duration_s exceeds 7200")
    # 409: valid request, fights current state. Retrying unchanged won't help.
    if store.exists(body["audio_id"]):
        raise HTTPException(409, "transcript already exists for this audio_id")
    job = queue.enqueue(body)                 # async work -> 202, never 201
    # Location tells the client WHERE to poll; 202 without it is a dead end.
    response.headers["Location"] = f"/v1/jobs/{job.id}"
    return {"job_id": job.id, "status": "queued",
            "status_url": f"/v1/jobs/{job.id}"}   # repeated in body for SDKs

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Four calls to that same POST /v1/transcripts, all for audio_id = aud_8831, plus one failure the handler never sees.

📥 POST /v1/transcripts   Content-Type: text/plain   {"audio_id":"aud_8831"}
    └─ ❌ 415 Unsupported Media Type      (rejected before any field is read)

📥 POST /v1/transcripts   Content-Type: application/json
   {"audio_id":"aud_8831","duration_s":9000}
    └─ ❌ 422 Unprocessable Content       (parsed fine — 9000 exceeds 7200)

📥 POST /v1/transcripts   {"audio_id":"aud_8831","duration_s":600}
    └─ ✅ 202 Accepted
       Location: /v1/jobs/job_4417
       body: {"job_id":"job_4417","status":"queued",
              "status_url":"/v1/jobs/job_4417"}

📥 POST /v1/transcripts   {"audio_id":"aud_8831","duration_s":600}   (again)
    └─ ⚠️ 409 Conflict                    (aud_8831 already has a transcript)

📥 POST /v1/transcripts   ... app pod OOM-killed mid-response ...
    └─ 🔥 502 Bad Gateway   emitted by the INGRESS, not by the handler
       (app access log has no entry — that absence is the signal)

  1. 415 fires before 422 on purpose. The first call sent text/plain; there is no meaningful field-level complaint to make about a body you refused to parse. Returning 422 there would send the client hunting through valid fields.

  2. 422 rather than 400 is a real signal. duration_s: 9000 is syntactically perfect JSON. 400 would tell the client "your bytes are malformed" and send them to debug their serialiser instead of their value.

  3. 202 rather than 201, because nothing was created yet. The transcript does not exist — a job does. Location: /v1/jobs/job_4417 plus status_url gives the client somewhere to poll; a 202 with {"ok": true} leaves it blind.

  4. 409 on the replay, 502 with no app log line. The repeat is a state conflict the client must resolve, not a server fault. The last case never reached the handler — the ingress got a reset mid-response, so the missing access-log entry is what separates an infrastructure 502 from an application 500.

10. When TO Use This

Reach for the precise code whenever a machine is the consumer — an SDK, a retry layer, a webhook receiver. The code is the only field they parse reliably, so precision buys correct client behaviour.

Use it when designing any async endpoint. The 201-versus-202 choice decides whether clients poll or assume completion; getting it wrong produces clients reading a resource that does not exist yet.

Use it during incident triage: split 5xx by code and emitting hop before touching anything. That split alone usually names the owner.

Use it when following redirects programmatically — 301/302 versus 307/308 decides whether the POST body survives.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't invent codes or overload obscure ones. A 418 or repurposed 299 is treated as its class by every intermediary and understood by nobody. Put the specificity in a machine-readable code field and keep the status honest.

Don't return 200 with an error payload. Common in GraphQL- and SOAP-shaped APIs, and it blinds every proxy, cache and dashboard in the path. If the protocol forces it, say so explicitly and build separate error metrics.

Don't use 403 where it leaks existence. Confirming another tenant's object exists is an enumeration oracle. GitHub returns 404 for private repos you cannot see — the right default for multi-tenant APIs.

Don't put semantics only in the code. "409" alone never tells a client which field conflicted. The code routes the response; the body explains it. Both, or the client guesses.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "4xx means the client did something wrong, 5xx means the server did."

✅ Reality: The useful reading is retryability, not blame. 4xx means this exact request fails identically, so change it or stop; 5xx means the same bytes may succeed later. 429 is a 4xx you should retry, and a 503 from an admission limiter is usually the client's own volume.

❌ Misconception: "301 and 302 differ only in how long the redirect lasts."

✅ Reality: Durability is real but secondary — the operational difference is method rewriting. Clients following a 301 or 302 turn a POST into a GET and drop the body, which is why 307 and 308 forbid it. Permanence bites separately: browsers cache 301s aggressively, so a mistaken one outlives the deploy that caused it.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning):

❌ I thought 502, 503 and 504 were three vaguely-equivalent ways of saying "the backend is unhappy", and I picked whichever the proxy happened to emit.

✅ They mark three points of failure on one path: the reply was unusable, there was nowhere to send it, or it was sent and never came back. Once I could name which meant "nothing was attempted", triage stopped being a guess — 503 sends me to health checks and pool membership, 504 to upstream latency, 502 to connection lifecycle.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Saying "500 for any server error". 500 is what you emit with nothing more specific. Reaching for it when the answer is 503 with Retry-After throws away the retry guidance the client needs.

Missing the 202 obligation. Saying "202 for async" without noting that the body must carry a polling URL, and that Location points at the job not the result, leaves the client with no way forward.

Treating 429 as a client bug. It is a retryable failure belonging in your backoff logic with Retry-After honoured, not an exception surfaced to the user. (→ Item 69)

Not knowing who emits what. Claiming your app returned a 503 when the mesh's admission limiter did sends the debugging conversation into the wrong codebase.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Item Value Context Source
Status classes 5 (1xx–5xx) The class is the contract; the code is detail RFC 9110 §15
Core codes, incl. 421 and 422 Defined in the base spec 422 = Unprocessable Content (renamed from Entity) RFC 9110 §15
428, 429, 431, 511 Additional codes Precondition Required, Too Many Requests, headers too large, network auth RFC 6585
425 Too Early Reject replayable early data For TLS 1.3 0-RTT requests RFC 8470
507 Insufficient Storage WebDAV extension Server cannot store the representation RFC 4918
308 Permanent Redirect Method-preserving permanent 307's permanent twin RFC 7538
Redirect-follow limit 20 hops Browsers and most clients then error out Fetch Standard — verify against your HTTP client's default
Retry-After format Seconds or an HTTP-date Both are legal; parse both MDN Retry-After

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Choosing a code costs nothing, but the code chosen drives client latency: a 503 with Retry-After: 30 prevents a hot retry loop that a bare 500 invites.
💰 Cost Correct 4xx codes stop clients from retrying doomed requests, which is direct compute saved on your side and theirs — most visible on expensive endpoints.
🎯 Quality Precise codes are the difference between an SDK that recovers automatically and one that surfaces a stack trace. This is the largest lever on perceived API quality.
📈 Scale Per-code, per-hop metric series cost more cardinality than one 5xx counter — and are worth it. Cardinality risk is in the labels (path, tenant), not the code itself.
🔧 Ops Complexity A consistent error contract is a compatibility surface you must version and cannot silently change; the discipline is ongoing, not a one-off.

16. Real World Usage

GitHub's REST API returns 404 rather than 403 for private repositories you cannot see, refusing to confirm existence. It is the reference example of treating 4xx as an information-leak surface.

AWS S3 signals throttling with 503 SlowDown, and the SDKs treat it as retryable with exponential backoff and jitter — the pattern AWS documented in its architecture blog. (→ Item 68)

Envoy emits 503 with response-flag annotations such as no-healthy-upstream, and 504 on upstream timeout — which is why mesh-fronted services see 5xx codes that never appear in application logs. Cloudflare adds its own 520–526 range for edge failures, precisely because 502 was too coarse to triage.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • HTTP methods & their contracts (Item 57) — 405 and redirect method-preservation only make sense against these.

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — the retry decision 4xx and 5xx feed. Read this first.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • Choosing the right status code (Item 60) — this procedure applied to specific API design cases.

  • Timeouts, retries & backoff (Item 68) — 429, 503 and Retry-After are that policy's inputs.

  • Rate limiting (Item 69) — 429 in operational detail, with quota headers.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • 200-with-error-envelope (GraphQL-style) — only when the transport cannot express per-field errors; costs you every proxy and dashboard signal.

  • gRPC status codes — a parallel 17-code space with a defined HTTP mapping; choose it when both ends are gRPC.

  • Custom error_code field only — a supplement, never a replacement: intermediaries cannot read your body.

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • ETags and preconditions (Item 61) — the source of 304, 412 and 428.

  • HTTP caching (Item 62) — which codes are cacheable; 404 and 410 are, by default, which surprises people.

  • Idempotency keys (Item 67) — 409 is what a key conflict returns; a 504 on a write is the ambiguity keys absorb.

19. System Design Application

The error contract has a real placement question: which hop is allowed to emit which class. Application code owns 2xx, 4xx and 500. The edge and mesh own 502, 503 and 504. Anything else is a bug — an app returning 502 usually means it is proxying something and hiding that fact, and an edge returning 422 means a WAF is reading bodies it should not be reading.

Placement drives the header contract too. Retry-After on a 503 must come from whatever component knows the recovery time — the admission or rate limiter, not a hardcoded edge value. A gateway inventing Retry-After: 60 when capacity returns in 3 seconds costs a minute of availability per event.

Monitoring follows directly. Never build a combined 5xx rate. Emit separate series per code, labelled by emitting hop, because each has a different owner and a different first check:

Series Alert on First check
http_5xx{code=500} Rate vs baseline App exception logs, recent deploy
http_5xx{code=502,hop=ingress} Any sustained rate Pod restarts, keep-alive timeout mismatch
http_5xx{code=503,hop=mesh} Any sustained rate Health checks, pool size, concurrency limits
http_5xx{code=504,hop=ingress} p99 upstream latency Upstream latency, proxy timeout budget
http_4xx{code=429} Rate and per-tenant skew Quota config, one noisy client

For SLOs, the availability numerator counts 5xx only. Counting 4xx means one misbehaving client's malformed requests burn your error budget, and you will end up excluding them mid-incident under pressure. 429 is the arguable case: it is your system deliberately refusing work, so track it as a separate saturation SLI rather than folding it into availability.

  • The registry — MDN: HTTP response status codes

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one question separating 401 from 403? Would different credentials help? Yes ⇒ 401. No ⇒ 403.
The one question separating 409 from 422? Could this same request succeed after state changes? Yes ⇒ 409.
Which header MUST accompany 401? WWW-Authenticate — mandatory in RFC 9110, routinely dropped.
Why 404 instead of 403 for another tenant's object? 403 confirms the resource exists. That is an enumeration oracle.
412 vs 428? 412 = your If-Match is stale. 428 = you sent none, refused.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Day before interview — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Picking a code is five yes/no questions, not a lookup. Did the bytes parse — no is 400, parsed but meaningless is 422. Would different credentials help — yes is 401, no is 403. Does 403 leak that the resource exists — then 404 instead. Would this succeed after state changed — that is 409, not 422. This client's quota or everyone's outage — 429 versus 503. Answer those five and the code falls out, and every retry layer downstream behaves.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through the confusable pairs — what single question separates each one?

🎯 Really testing: whether you carry a decision procedure or a memorised table you reach into and hope.

400 vs 422 — did the bytes parse? Unparseable JSON, a truncated body, a bad content encoding: 400, because the server never reached the fields. Valid JSON whose email field holds "tuesday", or a business-rule violation: 422 Unprocessable Content, syntactically fine and semantically wrong. Plenty of APIs collapse both into 400 and that is defensible; doing both inside one API is not, because the client's handler is then branching on a coin flip.

401 vs 403 — would different credentials help? Yes means 401, and RFC 9110 makes WWW-Authenticate mandatory on it, the half people drop. No means 403: identity established, permission refused, re-authenticating wasted. 403 vs 404 — may the caller know this resource exists at all?

409 vs 422 — would this exact request succeed later, after other state changed? Yes is 409 Conflict: an edit conflict, a duplicate unique key, a version mismatch. No is 422 — wrong against every possible state. 429 vs 503 — this caller's quota, or the whole server? (→ Item 59 for the catalogue.)

Tier 2 — Trade-off

You're designing a multi-tenant API. Another tenant asks for GET /docs/d_88. 403 or 404?

📍 Seen in the wild: GitHub returns 404 for private repositories you cannot see; the pattern is now the default expectation for any multi-tenant SaaS.

404, and I'd say so before the reasoning: a 403 on an object the caller was never meant to know about confirms that d_88 exists. Hand an attacker a loop over the ID space and each 403 is a bit of information — an enumeration oracle, and with sequential IDs it leaks volume too, since the highest ID returning 403 is roughly your document count. A 404 answers identically whether the document exists or not, so the loop learns nothing.

The trade is worth naming unprompted: debugging gets worse for legitimate users. A ticket saying "it 404s but I can see it in the UI" is genuinely ambiguous — wrong tenant, revoked grant, or deleted. Pair it with a request ID in body and header, log the true reason against that ID, and support resolves it in one lookup. The discriminating information never crosses the wire, so the security property survives.

The flip condition: inside a single trust boundary — an internal admin tool, or an org where every member may see the resource list — 403 is better, since it tells the operator the object is there and a grant is missing.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Status codes are a client contract. What breaks at scale when the code is wrong?

🎯 Really testing: whether you see the code as an input to somebody else's automated control loop rather than a label on a log line.

Every retry layer branches on the class without reading your body: 4xx means this exact request fails again, 5xx means the same bytes might work later. Return 500 for what is really a 400 and you have told a generic retry layer to keep resending a permanently-failing request. Across a fleet, with retries at browser, gateway and service client, that multiplies to 27 attempts per user action worst case — and the 500 rate feeding your circuit breakers is now dominated by requests that were never the server's fault. (→ Item 68)

The reverse error is quieter and costs availability: 400 or 422 for a transient dependency failure tells clients to stop permanently, so a blip backoff would have absorbed becomes a hard user-visible error.

Two codes cross the retry line and both need Retry-After. Emit 503 for a per-client quota and every well-behaved client backs off, hiding which tenant caused it; emit 429 during a real outage and clients go audit their own quota config. The detection signal is the attempt-to-unique-request ratio per code — a 4xx above 1 means somebody is retrying what you told them was hopeless.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the error body that makes these distinctions machine-readable for a public API.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat the error surface as a versioned contract with a compatibility guarantee.

One body shape everywhere, RFC 9457 problem-details style, served as application/problem+json: a stable machine-readable code, the numeric status, a human title and detail, and a request ID. Clients branch on code, never on prose, which keeps the prose free to change. The status carries the coarse decision — retry or don't — while code says which decision produced it, so conflict.version_mismatch and conflict.duplicate_key are both 409 but handled differently.

Validation errors need a second level. A 422 with one detail string forces clients to regex your English; an errors array of {pointer, code, detail} lets a form highlight the offending input. Return every failing field at once — one per round trip trains users to hate you.

The 4xx body is where you leak. Never confirm a resource the caller may not access, never echo internal IDs, table names, upstream hostnames or stack traces; those live behind the request ID, in your logs. Version it like any surface: adding a code is additive, redefining one is breaking, so codes get deprecated with a window instead. (Hop placement and monitoring belong to Item 59.)

4. Quick Comparison Table

Pair The deciding question Left Right
400 vs 422 Did the bytes parse? 400 — unparseable JSON, bad encoding, missing framing 422 — parsed and understood, meaning is wrong
401 vs 403 Would different credentials help? 401 — MUST carry WWW-Authenticate 403 — authenticated, not permitted
404 vs 403 May the caller know it exists? 404 — hides existence, needs a request ID 403 — safe only inside one trust boundary
409 vs 422 Could the same request succeed later? 409 — fights current state (edit conflict, duplicate key) 422 — wrong against any state
429 vs 503 This client, or everyone? 429 — this caller's quota; others fine 503 — server down for all
412 vs 428 Did they send If-Match? 412 — sent, and it is now stale 428 — none sent, server refuses to guess

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

One clerk, one counter, and every way your form comes back across it.

You slide a form under the glass. Your handwriting is unreadable — 400, she can't start. You rewrite it neatly, but in the box marked amount you've written "Tuesday" — 422, legible and meaningless. She asks for your badge; you have none, and she points at the sign naming which badge to get — 401 with WWW-Authenticate. You return with a valid badge, wrong colour for this floor — 403. You ask about room 12 on a floor you aren't cleared for; she says flatly that no such room exists — 404, hiding it on purpose, and slides you a ticket number.

Later your form is perfect, but someone booked that room an hour ago — 409. You try again quoting the version off your photocopied sheet; the sheet has moved on — 412. From then on she refuses any form without a version — 428. Thirty forms against a limit of twenty: come back at 2pm — 429 with Retry-After. Next morning the office is shut — 503.

Story beat Mechanism
Unreadable handwriting 400 — parse failure, no fields ever reached
"Tuesday" in the amount box 422 — syntax fine, semantics wrong
No badge, sign says which to get 401 plus the mandatory WWW-Authenticate
Valid badge, wrong colour 403 — authenticated, not permitted
"No such room" for a floor you can't enter 404 chosen deliberately to hide existence
The slip with a ticket number The request ID that makes 404-hiding debuggable
Room booked an hour ago 409 — conflicts with current state
Your photocopy is out of date 412 — If-Match no longer matches the ETag
She now demands a version on every form 428 — lost updates become impossible, not merely detectable
Your thirty-form limit, come back at 2pm 429 plus Retry-After — this caller only
Whole office shut 503 — everyone, not you

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No math — an ordered sequence of yes/no tests, where the order is load-bearing.

  THE FIVE QUESTIONS, IN ORDER

  1. Did the bytes parse?                 no -> 400        yes -> keep going
  2. Would other credentials help?        yes -> 401       no  -> question 3
  3. May the caller know it exists?       no  -> 404       yes -> 403
  4. Is it this caller, or everyone?      caller -> 429    everyone -> 503
  5. Could it succeed after state moved?  yes -> 409       no  -> 422

  PRECONDITIONS sit between 4 and 5:
     If-Match required but absent  -> 428   (lost update made impossible)
     If-Match sent but stale       -> 412   (lost update merely detected)

  409 says "something about the state fights you."
  412 says "the state moved, and here is exactly which version you missed."

Order is what makes the codes informative. Permission is decided before existence, so you never confirm a resource you would not serve; parsing before field semantics, since you cannot complain about fields in a body you could not read; preconditions before the generic conflict check, because 412 is the precise form of 409 and precision always wins.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The code is the only part of your error every intermediary reads. SDK retry policies, circuit breakers, CDN negative caching and alert rules branch on it without opening the body, so a mislabelled failure changes systems you do not own, in ways that surface only under load.

The security half fails silently. A 403 where 404 belonged is not an outage; it is an information disclosure that works perfectly and appears on no dashboard. You find it in a pentest report months later, by which time clients depend on the leak.

8. Code / Pseudocode Example

A FastAPI update endpoint whose whole job is picking codes. This is the example traced in Section 9.

@app.put("/v1/docs/{doc_id}")
def update(doc_id: str, body: dict, req: Request, caller=Depends(auth)):
    doc = store.get(doc_id)
    # 404, never 403: a 403 here confirms another tenant's doc exists. The
    # request ID is how support recovers the real reason, from the logs.
    if doc is None or doc.tenant != caller.tenant:
        raise problem(404, "not_found", request_id=req.state.rid)
    # 428 BEFORE 412: refusing blind writes makes lost updates impossible.
    if "if-match" not in req.headers:
        raise problem(428, "precondition_required", detail="send If-Match")
    # 412, not 409: the server knows EXACTLY which version they missed.
    if req.headers["if-match"] != doc.etag:
        raise problem(412, "etag_stale", current_etag=doc.etag)
    # 422, not 400: the JSON parsed fine — the VALUE is wrong. The pointer
    # lets the client highlight the input instead of regexing prose.
    if not EMAIL_RE.match(body.get("owner_email", "")):
        raise problem(422, "invalid_field", pointer="/owner_email")
    if doc.locked_by_review:   # 409: valid content, fights CURRENT state
        raise problem(409, "locked_pending_review")
    return store.put(doc_id, body, caller)

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Six calls to PUT /v1/docs/d_9f2c. The document belongs to tenant t_42; its ETag is "v7".

📥 PUT /v1/docs/d_9f2c    caller tenant = t_09    (document belongs to t_42)
    └─ ❌ 404 not_found   {"request_id":"rq_5a1c"}   ← NOT 403: existence hidden

📥 PUT /v1/docs/d_9f2c    caller tenant = t_42    (no If-Match header)
    └─ ❌ 428 precondition_required   "send If-Match"

📥 PUT /v1/docs/d_9f2c    If-Match: "v6"          (someone else wrote v7)
    └─ ❌ 412 etag_stale   {"current_etag":"v7"}   ← names the exact version

📥 PUT /v1/docs/d_9f2c    If-Match: "v7"
   {"owner_email":"tuesday"}
    └─ ❌ 422 invalid_field   {"pointer":"/owner_email"}   ← parsed fine

📥 PUT /v1/docs/d_9f2c    If-Match: "v7"   {"owner_email":"a@b.io"}
    └─ ⚠️ 409 locked_pending_review        ← same body will succeed later

📥 PUT /v1/docs/d_9f2c    If-Match: "v7"   (review closed, lock released)
    └─ ✅ 200 OK   ETag: "v8"

  1. 404 rather than 403, with a request ID to make it survivable. The response is byte-identical to a genuinely missing document, so a loop over the ID space learns nothing. rq_5a1c is the only thread back to the true reason, which lives in the log where an attacker cannot reach it.

  2. 428 fires before 412 by design. Refusing the write outright when If-Match is absent converts lost updates from detectable to impossible. 412 is weaker — it helps only clients that already opted in.

  3. 412 rather than 409 because the server can be precise. Both mean "the state moved under you", but 412 hands back current_etag: "v7", so the client re-reads one version instead of diffing blind. (→ Item 61)

  4. 422 then 409 separate wrong content from wrong moment. owner_email: "tuesday" is wrong against every state, so retrying is pointless until the client edits it. The lock is the opposite, and the sixth call proves it — identical body, review closed, 200 with a fresh ETag.

10. When TO Use This

Apply the full procedure on any endpoint an SDK or another service calls. Machines reliably parse the code and nothing else, so precision separates automatic recovery from a stack trace.

Apply it hardest on multi-tenant read paths, where 403-versus-404 is a security boundary rather than a style preference, and a wrong call stays invisible until an audit.

Apply it on write paths with concurrent editors: the 428/412/409 trio is the whole optimistic-concurrency story, and the choice tells a client to re-read, merge or wait. (→ Item 61)

Apply it when you own a rate limiter or admission controller — where 429 and 503 get confused, and a wrong choice reshapes client backoff.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't split 400 and 422 if you cannot enforce the split. Half the handlers using 422 and half 400 for the same failure is worse than always using 400 — clients can code against a blunt rule, not an inconsistent one. Pick one, then lint for it.

Don't return 404-for-hiding to a caller who already knows the resource exists. A document shared yesterday and revoked today reads as deleted. 403 is correct there: existence is no longer the secret, access is.

Don't reach for 409 when a precondition would give you 412. 409 says "something conflicted" and leaves the client to work out what; 412 with the current ETag names the version missed. Vagueness is paid in round trips.

Don't emit 503 for anything scoped to one caller. Every well-behaved client backs off on a 503, so a per-tenant limit dressed as 503 spreads one tenant's problem across the fleet. (→ Item 69)

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "422 is just a more specific 400 — use whichever reads better."

✅ Reality: They send the client to two different places. 400 says your bytes are malformed — go look at the serialiser and the encoding. 422 says the bytes parsed and one value was wrong — go look at the field. Choose by whether the parser succeeded, not by taste; if you cannot hold that line across every handler, collapse to 400 deliberately and document it.

❌ Misconception: "403 is the secure response for an unauthorised request."

✅ Reality: 403 admits the resource exists. For anything tenant-scoped, that admission is the leak — an attacker iterating IDs reads 403 as "found one". A 404 answers identically whether or not the object is real, and is the right default unless existence is already known to that caller.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning):

❌ I treated the choice as cosmetic — 400 for anything the client got wrong, 500 for everything else — since the body carried the real message anyway.

✅ The body is read by humans; the code is read by retry layers, circuit breakers, CDNs and alert rules that never open it. Once I saw the code as an input to somebody else's control loop, the pairs stopped being trivia: a wrong 500 makes fleets retry doomed requests, a wrong 403 gives away existence.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Getting 401 right but forgetting WWW-Authenticate. RFC 9110 makes it mandatory, and it tells the client which scheme to retry with. "401 means unauthenticated" without it is the half-answer interviewers listen for.

Claiming 404-for-hiding without naming the cost. The security argument is easy; the senior version names the debugging damage and pays it off with a request ID.

Treating 409 and 412 as synonyms. 412 exists because a precondition let the server say which version you missed. Collapsing them discards what the client needs to avoid a re-read.

Explaining 429 versus 503 without Retry-After on both. Both are retryable, and both are useless to a backoff loop left guessing the interval. Naming the header — and that it accepts seconds or an HTTP-date — is the difference between theory and having shipped it. (→ Item 68)

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Item Value Context Source
WWW-Authenticate on 401 MUST Not optional; the most-dropped requirement in the pair RFC 9110 §15.5.2
403 Forbidden No obligation to reveal the reason Spec explicitly permits 404 instead to hide existence RFC 9110 §15.5.4
422 Unprocessable Content Renamed from "Entity" Semantically invalid, syntactically fine RFC 9110 §15.5.21
412 Precondition Failed Triggered by If-Match / If-Unmodified-Since The precise form of a state conflict RFC 9110 §15.5.13
428 Precondition Required Server demands a conditional request Turns lost updates from detectable to impossible RFC 6585
429 Too Many Requests Per-client quota exceeded Defined alongside 428 in the same RFC RFC 6585
Retry-After format Seconds or an HTTP-date Both legal on 429 and 503; parse both MDN Retry-After
Problem-details media type application/problem+json The standard error body shape RFC 9457
Retry amplification, 3 layers × 3 attempts 27× worst case Why a wrong 500 is expensive at fleet scale Derived (3³)

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency The choice costs nothing to make, but drives client latency: 429 with Retry-After: 30 prevents a hot loop that a bare 500 invites, and 412 with the current ETag saves a re-read round trip that a bare 409 forces.
💰 Cost Correct 4xx stops clients retrying doomed requests — compute saved on both sides. The 404-for-hiding choice costs support time instead, paid in tickets rather than CPU.
🎯 Quality Field-level 422 bodies with JSON Pointers are what let a UI highlight the wrong input. This is the single largest lever on how an API feels to integrate against.
📈 Scale Precision matters more as the client fleet grows: one wrong code is one confused developer at ten clients, and a coordinated retry storm at ten thousand.
🔧 Ops Complexity Consistency has to be enforced, not intended — a lint rule or a shared problem() helper. Every handler that hand-rolls its own code is a future inconsistency.

16. Real World Usage

GitHub's REST API returns 404 for private repositories you cannot see, and documents the choice rather than leaving it an accident — the canonical case of treating 403/404 as a security control.

Stripe returns 409 when an idempotency key is reused with a different body: a state conflict rather than bad content, and a clean illustration of the 409-versus-422 test. (→ Item 67)

Kubernetes' API server returns 409 on a resource-version mismatch — optimistic concurrency as in 412, expressed through the body instead of an ETag header.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • Status codes — the practical map (Item 59) — the catalogue this note decides against. Read this first.

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — the retry contract that makes a wrong class expensive.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • ETags and preconditions (Item 61) — where 412 and 428 come from, in mechanism detail.

  • Timeouts, retries & backoff (Item 68) — the client loop your code choice programs.

  • Idempotency keys (Item 67) — key-reuse conflicts are the cleanest real 409.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Collapse 400 and 422 into 400 — when you cannot enforce the split across every handler; consistency beats precision.

  • gRPC status codes — 17 codes with a defined HTTP mapping; FAILED_PRECONDITION versus ABORTED is the 422/409 decision renamed.

  • Problem details only, status always 200 — reject it: intermediaries never read your body.

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • HTTP caching (Item 62) — 404 is cacheable by default, so a hiding-404 can outlive the grant change that caused it.

  • Request IDs — what makes a deliberately uninformative 404 supportable.
