notes.title: Headers That Matter

headings.text: Walk me through ETag, If-None-Match and If-Match — they look like the same mechanism.
A client reports lost updates on a shared record. Which header do you reach for, and what breaks if you don't?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • ETag and preconditions — MDN: ETag

  • Retry signalling — MDN: Retry-After

  • Normative field definitions — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, §8 & §13

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which header prevents lost updates, and what does it return? If-Match with an ETag → 412 Precondition Failed on conflict.
If-None-Match vs If-Match? If-None-Match = caching, gives 304. If-Match = concurrency, gives 412.
Why is X-Forwarded-For untrustworthy? Clients can forge it; only the value your own proxy appended is real.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Headers are where most of HTTP's real behaviour lives. Four groups matter: negotiation — Content-Type and Accept decide what representation you get; auth — Authorization carries the bearer token or scheme; caching and concurrency — Cache-Control, ETag, If-None-Match for freshness and If-Match for optimistic locking; and operational — Retry-After, X-Request-ID, X-Forwarded-For. The one people miss is If-Match. Idempotency stops duplicate writes, but it does nothing about two clients overwriting each other, and that gap is exactly what preconditions close.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through ETag, If-None-Match and If-Match — they look like the same mechanism.

They share a token and nothing else. An ETag is an opaque server-generated version identifier for a representation — a hash, a row version, a storage generation number. If-None-Match is the caching direction: the client sends the ETag it holds and the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body if it still matches, saving the payload but not the round trip. If-Match is the concurrency direction: the client sends the ETag it read, and the server executes the write only if the resource is still at that version, otherwise 412 Precondition Failed. (→ Item 62)

Validator strength matters. A weak validator, written W/"abc", means semantically equivalent — fine for cache revalidation, not acceptable for If-Match, which requires strong comparison because "close enough" is no basis for permitting a write. If-Unmodified-Since is the timestamp fallback and weaker still: one-second granularity makes two writes inside the same second indistinguishable, so use ETags on contended resources.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A client reports lost updates on a shared record. Which header do you reach for, and what breaks if you don't?

📍 Seen in the wild: two support agents editing one ticket; the second save silently discards the first agent's note.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know idempotency and concurrency are different problems with different fixes.

If-Match with a strong ETag. The read returns ETag: "v7"; the write sends If-Match: "v7"; the server compares under the same lock or transaction that performs the write and returns 412 if the version moved. The client then re-reads, rebases its change and retries — or, for a form, shows a diff rather than a blind overwrite. The critical implementation detail is that the compare and the write must be atomic; a read-check-then-write handler races exactly the way it did without the header.

What breaks without it is invisible, which is why it goes unfixed for years. Both writes return 200, both clients believe they succeeded, and the earlier field value is simply gone — no error, no log line, no alert. Idempotency keys do not help here: they deduplicate the same operation, not two different operations racing. (→ Item 58) The flip condition is contention. Under low contention, last-write-wins is cheaper and the 412 retry loop is dead code; adopt preconditions when the resource is genuinely shared or when a lost field is a compliance problem rather than an annoyance.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Purpose Header Direction What it decides
Negotiation Content-Type Both Media type of this body
Negotiation Accept Request Media types the client will take; drives 406
Auth Authorization Request Scheme plus credentials; Bearer <jwt> in practice
Caching Cache-Control Both Storage and freshness policy (→ Item 62)
Caching ETag / If-None-Match Response / Request Revalidation → 304 Not Modified
Concurrency ETag / If-Match Response / Request Optimistic locking → 412 Precondition Failed
Operational Retry-After Response Seconds or HTTP-date; on 429 and 503
Operational X-Request-ID Both Correlation across hops and logs
Operational X-Forwarded-For / Forwarded Request Original client IP — client-forgeable

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No math — the mechanism is a workflow. The precondition path is the one worth internalising, because it is where the two If- headers diverge.

The load-bearing box is the one that says "under the same lock as the write". Compare outside the transaction and you have reimplemented the race you were fixing, with a header that makes reviewers assume it is handled.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't trust X-Forwarded-For as sent. It is a client-writable list, so a caller can prepend any address. Trust only the value appended by a proxy you control, counted from the rightmost entry inward, and only when the connection came from a known proxy IP. Otherwise per-IP rate limits and audit logs are trivially forgeable. RFC 7239's Forwarded is the standardised replacement, with identical hop-count discipline.

Don't put secrets in custom headers and assume they're private. Proxies, access logs and APM agents record header values by default. Authorization is redacted by most tooling because it is well known; X-Api-Key is not.

Don't send Retry-After you can't honour. On a 429 or 503 it is a promise clients back off against. A fixed value across all callers synchronises every retry into one thundering herd at the same instant — vary it, or return a jittered value. (→ Item 69)

Don't use If-Unmodified-Since where writes are frequent. One-second granularity cannot separate two updates in the same second, so the precondition passes and the update is lost anyway.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "If-Match and If-None-Match are two spellings of the same cache check."

✅ Reality: They serve opposite goals and return different codes. If-None-Match on a GET saves bandwidth via 304 and tolerates weak validators. If-Match on a write is optimistic concurrency control, requires strong comparison, and returns 412 so the client knows its change was refused — using the wrong one leaves you with either useless caching or silent data loss.

❌ Misconception: "X-Request-ID is just for pretty logs."

✅ Reality: It is the join key that makes multi-hop debugging possible — without one, correlating a client error with a gateway log and three service logs means guessing by timestamp. Generate it at the edge if absent, propagate it on every outbound call, and return it so a user can quote it in a ticket.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • HTTP methods & their contracts (Item 57) — the requests these headers annotate.

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — the gap If-Match fills.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • HTTP caching (Item 62) — Cache-Control, ETag and Vary in operational depth. Read immediately after this.

  • Choosing the right status code (Item 60) — 304, 406, 412 and 428 are precondition outcomes.

  • Rate limiting (Item 69) — Retry-After and the per-IP trust question meet here.

  • Distributed tracing (Item 161) — X-Request-ID generalised into trace context propagation.

notes.title: HTTP Caching

headings.text: Go through the Cache-Control directives that actually change behaviour.
Product needs deploys visible within a minute. Short TTLs, or versioned URLs?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Caching guide — MDN: HTTP caching

  • Directive reference — MDN: Cache-Control

  • Normative model — RFC 9111: HTTP Caching

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
no-cache vs no-store? no-cache = store but revalidate first. no-store = never write it down.
private vs public? private = browser only. public = shared caches (CDN, proxy) may store it.
What does a successful revalidation return? 304 Not Modified — headers only, no body, cache entry refreshed.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Caching runs on two clocks. Freshness is Cache-Control: max-age — while the response is fresh, a cache serves it with no network call at all. Once stale, the cache revalidates: it sends If-None-Match with the ETag and gets back a 304 with no body, or a 200 with fresh content. s-maxage targets shared caches separately from browsers, private versus public draws the shared-cache boundary, and Vary tells the cache which request headers form part of the key. Get private wrong on a personalised response and a CDN serves one user's data to another.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Go through the Cache-Control directives that actually change behaviour.

max-age=N sets freshness lifetime in seconds for every cache; s-maxage=N overrides it for shared caches only, which is how you keep a CDN copy for an hour while browsers hold it for a minute. no-cache still permits storage but forbids reuse without successful revalidation — it is the "always ask, usually get a cheap 304" setting. no-store is the different one: never write the response to disk or memory, which is what you want for a bank statement. must-revalidate closes the loophole where a cache serves stale content when the origin is unreachable.

The performance directives are newer and underused. immutable tells the browser not to revalidate even on reload, which is correct only for content-hashed asset URLs. stale-while-revalidate=N serves the stale copy instantly and refreshes in the background, converting a revalidation round trip into zero user-visible latency. stale-if-error=N serves stale content when the origin returns 5xx, which turns a hard outage into slightly old data. ETag/If-None-Match and the coarser Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since supply the validators all of this depends on. (→ Item 61)

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Product needs deploys visible within a minute. Short TTLs, or versioned URLs?

📍 Seen in the wild: "we shipped the fix an hour ago and customers still see the old bundle".

🎯 Really testing: whether you know invalidation is a naming problem before it is a TTL problem.

For static assets I take versioned URLs every time: build a content hash into the filename, serve it with max-age=31536000, immutable, and never invalidate anything — a new deploy produces new URLs, so the old entries simply stop being requested. The only short-TTL surface left is the HTML that references those URLs, typically no-cache so it revalidates on every load and costs one 304. That combination gives instant deploy visibility and near-perfect cache hit rates simultaneously, which no single TTL can.

The flip condition is whether you control the URL. API responses, user-generated content and third-party embeds have identifiers you cannot rewrite per version, so you fall back to short s-maxage plus stale-while-revalidate to hide the revalidation cost, or to explicit CDN purge if the platform supports it. Purge is the option I reject by default: it is eventually consistent across PoPs, has no useful failure signal, and turns every content change into a distributed-systems problem you own.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Directive / header Who it binds Effect Use when
max-age=N All caches Fresh for N seconds, no network call Anything with a known lifetime
s-maxage=N Shared caches only Overrides max-age at CDN/proxy CDN holds longer than the browser
no-cache All caches Store, but revalidate before every use Content that changes unpredictably
no-store All caches Never write it down Statements, tokens, PII
private Shared caches Browser may store, CDN must not Any per-user response
public Shared caches Storable even with Authorization Shared static assets
must-revalidate All caches No stale serving when origin is down Correctness beats availability
immutable Browsers Skip revalidation even on reload Content-hashed asset URLs
stale-while-revalidate=N All caches Serve stale, refresh in background Hide revalidation latency
stale-if-error=N All caches Serve stale on origin 5xx Outage resilience
Vary All caches Adds request headers to the cache key Accept-Encoding, Authorization

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No math — the mechanism is a workflow. Every cache in the path runs this same freshness decision, independently.

Note where the savings differ. A fresh hit costs zero round trips; a 304 still costs a full RTT and saves only the body. So on a small JSON response over a 70 ms link, revalidation saves almost nothing — the win is entirely in the freshness branch, which is why max-age tuning beats validator tuning for small payloads. (→ Item 6)

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't cache anything personalised without private. A response rendered with one user's name and a public or default policy can be stored by a CDN and served to the next requester of that URL. The detection signal is users reporting someone else's data — treat it as an incident, not a bug.

Don't ship Vary: * or a Vary on a high-cardinality header. Vary: User-Agent multiplies the cache key across thousands of UA strings and drives the hit rate toward zero while consuming storage. Keep it to Accept-Encoding and, where responses differ per credential, Authorization.

Don't rely on CDN purge as your invalidation strategy. Purges propagate asynchronously across PoPs with no consistency guarantee and no per-PoP receipt. Design so most content never needs purging, and keep purge for emergencies.

Don't cache error responses on default settings. A 500 or a 404 stored with a long TTL keeps serving after the origin recovers. Set explicit short lifetimes for error status codes, or no-store them.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "no-cache means the response isn't cached."

✅ Reality: no-cache means store it, but revalidate with the origin before every reuse — the cache still holds the body and usually gets a cheap 304 back. no-store is the directive that forbids writing it down at all. Using no-cache for a bank statement leaves the document sitting in a disk cache; using no-store for a homepage throws away a free 304.

❌ Misconception: "If I set max-age, everything downstream will respect it."

✅ Reality: A response with Authorization is not stored by shared caches unless you explicitly say public or s-maxage, and Vary mismatches quietly turn hits into misses. Verify with the response's Age header and the CDN's hit-ratio metric rather than assuming the directive took effect.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — which methods are cacheable at all.

  • Headers that matter (Item 61) — ETag, If-None-Match and Cache-Control as fields.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • CDNs and edge caching (Item 110) — this model deployed across PoPs. Read immediately after this.

  • Choosing the right status code (Item 60) — why 304 is not an error and must carry no body.

  • Content negotiation (Item 63) — where Vary correctness is decided.

  • Latency vs bandwidth (Item 6) — why a fresh hit and a 304 are not comparable savings.

notes.title: Cookies and Cookie Attributes

headings.text: What does each attribute actually change, and which ones are security controls?
Single-page app talking to your API: HttpOnly session cookie, or a bearer token in Authorization?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Mechanism and attributes — MDN: Using HTTP cookies

  • Every attribute, normatively described — MDN: Set-Cookie

  • How cookies sit in HTTP's state model — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does HttpOnly actually stop? document.cookie reads — so XSS cannot exfiltrate the session value.
SameSite=None requires what? Secure. Browsers reject None over plain HTTP.
Cookies vs bearer tokens in one line? Cookies auto-send (CSRF risk); bearer tokens don't (storage risk).

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A cookie is server-set state that the browser attaches automatically to every matching request — matching meaning the Domain and Path line up, and Secure and SameSite permit it. That automatic attachment is the whole story: it's why sessions are effortless, and it's why cross-site request forgery exists at all, since an attacker's page can trigger a request that carries your session without ever reading it. SameSite=Lax is the default mitigation, HttpOnly blocks script access, and __Host- locks scope. Which leaves the question interviewers actually want: why not just use a bearer token?

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What does each attribute actually change, and which ones are security controls?

HttpOnly removes the cookie from document.cookie, so a successful XSS can still ride the session but cannot copy it out to an attacker's server — the difference between a session hijacked for as long as the page is open and one replayed for two weeks. Secure refuses to send over plain HTTP. SameSite=Strict withholds the cookie on every cross-site request, Lax allows it only on top-level navigations with safe methods, None restores old behaviour and requires Secure. Those four are security controls.

Domain, Path, Max-Age and Expires are scope and lifetime, not security. Domain only widens: setting Domain=example.com shares the cookie with every subdomain, including one you don't control, which is the standard subdomain-takeover escalation path. Path is trivially bypassed by an attacker who can load an iframe. The __Host- prefix is the real fix — a browser only accepts it when the cookie is Secure, Path=/, and carries no Domain, pinning it to exactly one origin. __Secure- requires only Secure.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Single-page app talking to your API: HttpOnly session cookie, or a bearer token in Authorization?

Default to the HttpOnly cookie with SameSite=Lax and the __Host- prefix, because the two attack classes are not symmetric. XSS against localStorage yields a long-lived token the attacker replays from their own machine at leisure; CSRF against a cookie yields blind, same-origin-only requests, and SameSite=Lax already blocks the cross-site POST that CSRF depends on. You're not eliminating risk, you're choosing which one you'd rather defend — and cookie risk is bounded by the browser, token risk isn't.

The condition that flips it: cross-origin or non-browser clients. Mobile apps, server-to-server callers and CLI tools have no cookie jar, and a third-party API on a different registrable domain needs SameSite=None; Secure, which discards the CSRF protection you were paying for. At that point a short-lived bearer token plus a refresh token held in an HttpOnly cookie is the honest split. Detection signal for a broken setup: session works on localhost, fails in staging — usually SameSite plus a missing Secure.

📍 Seen in the wild: teams add SameSite=None to fix a preview-deployment login bug, then ship it to production and silently disable CSRF protection everywhere.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name the trade-off honestly instead of reciting "never store tokens in localStorage".

4. Quick Comparison Table

HttpOnly cookie Bearer token in localStorage Token in memory only
Sent automatically Yes — by the browser No — app adds the header No
CSRF exposure Yes → mitigate with SameSite None None
XSS can read it No Yes — full exfiltration Only while the tab lives
Survives page reload Yes Yes No — needs silent re-auth
Works for mobile / server clients Poorly Yes Yes
Revocation Server-side session delete Needs a denylist or short TTL Short TTL

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Every branch above is evaluated by the browser before the request leaves, and none of it is visible to your server — a cookie that fails a check simply arrives absent, producing a 401 with no explanation. Debug by reading the request in devtools, not the server log. (→ Item 64)

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't use cookies for non-browser clients. A mobile app or service caller has no cookie jar and no SameSite notion; you'd be reimplementing a jar to get worse ergonomics than an Authorization header.

Don't put anything sensitive in the cookie value. A cookie is client-held storage: readable by the user, tamperable without a signature, and capped near 4 KB per cookie. Store an opaque session ID and keep the state server-side.

Don't set Domain to widen scope for convenience. Sharing a session cookie across *.example.com means every subdomain — including a forgotten CNAME pointing at a decommissioned vendor — can read it. Prefer __Host- and per-origin cookies.

Don't rely on SameSite as your only CSRF defence. It is browser-enforced, defaults vary by browser and version, and Lax still permits cross-site top-level GETs. Pair it with a synchroniser token or an origin check on state-changing methods. (→ Item 58)

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "HttpOnly protects against XSS."

✅ Reality: It protects against exfiltration of the cookie, not against XSS. Injected script still runs in the origin and can issue authenticated requests — the browser attaches the cookie for it. HttpOnly bounds the blast radius to the victim's live session; it does not stop the attack.

❌ Misconception: "Setting Path=/admin stops other pages from using the cookie."

✅ Reality: Path is a scoping convenience, not an isolation boundary. Any script in the same origin can navigate or fetch a URL under that path and cause the cookie to be sent. Only __Host- plus origin separation gives a real boundary.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — SameSite=Lax keys off exactly the safe-method distinction.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • CORS (Item 64) — credentialed cross-origin requests are where cookie rules and CORS rules collide. Read immediately after this.

  • Choosing the right status code (Item 60) — an absent cookie surfaces as 401 versus 403, and the difference is diagnostic.

  • HTTP caching (Item 62) — a response varying on a cookie must say so, or a shared cache leaks one user's page to another.

notes.title: CORS and Preflight Requests

headings.text: What exactly triggers a preflight, and what does it exchange?
A team wants Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on an internal API to "make CORS errors go away". Do you allow it?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The whole mechanism — MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

  • OPTIONS and method semantics — MDN: HTTP request methods

  • Header and method definitions — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Who enforces CORS? The browser. Servers only advertise; curl and Postman ignore it entirely.
Three preflight triggers? Non-GET/HEAD/POST method · non-simple Content-Type · any non-safelisted header.
Allow-Credentials: true forbids what? Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. You must echo one concrete origin.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

CORS is how a server tells the browser that a page from another origin is allowed to read its response. The key word is browser: the request usually reaches the server and executes, and the browser then withholds the response from JavaScript. Simple requests go straight through; anything with a custom header, a JSON content type, or a method beyond GET, HEAD or POST first triggers an OPTIONS preflight asking permission. That asymmetry explains the most common bug report in the industry — "it works in Postman but not in the browser" — and it's why CORS is not a server-side security control.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What exactly triggers a preflight, and what does it exchange?

Three conditions, any one of which is enough. First, a method other than GET, HEAD or POST — so every PUT, PATCH and DELETE preflights. Second, a Content-Type other than application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain — which means application/json, the default for every modern API, always preflights. Third, any request header outside the CORS-safelist, so a single Authorization or X-Request-Id is sufficient. The rule exists because those three shapes are the ones an HTML form could not have produced before CORS existed.

The preflight is an OPTIONS request carrying Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers, with no body and no credentials. The server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods, -Headers and optionally -Max-Age, which caps how long the browser may cache the decision — commonly clamped to a few hours, so a value of 7200 is a realistic ceiling. Only after that does the real request go. The measurable cost is one extra round trip per unique method-and-header combination per cache lifetime, which on a 70 ms RTT is 70 ms added to a cold call.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A team wants Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on an internal API to "make CORS errors go away". Do you allow it?

For a genuinely public, credential-free, read-only endpoint — a status page or a public dataset — * is fine and simplest. Everywhere else it's the wrong instinct, because it signals that CORS is being treated as a permission gate when it is only a browser-side read barrier. If that internal API is reachable from a user's browser and relies on cookies, * is not even legal: with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true the browser rejects the wildcard outright, so the fix that "made errors go away" will fail the moment credentials are added.

The workable pattern is an allowlist of exact origins, matched server-side and echoed into Access-Control-Allow-Origin, plus Vary: Origin on every such response. Skip the Vary and any shared cache or CDN in front will serve the first origin's cached response to a second origin, producing a CORS failure that reproduces only for some users and disappears on refresh. And say the quiet part in the interview: none of this protects the endpoint from a non-browser client — authentication and network policy do that. (→ Item 62)

📍 Seen in the wild: a reflect-any-origin regex like /example\.com/ that also matches evil-example.com.attacker.net.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know CORS relaxes the same-origin policy rather than enforcing anything.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Simple request Preflighted request Credentialed request
Extra round trip No Yes — one OPTIONS Yes, if also preflighted
Triggered by GET/HEAD/POST with simple Content-Type Other method, JSON body, or custom header credentials: 'include' or cookies
Allow-Origin: * legal Yes Yes No — must echo one origin
Needs Vary: Origin When echoing origins When echoing origins Always
Response readable by JS Only if Allow-Origin matches Only after preflight approves Also needs Allow-Credentials: true
Server still executes it Yes No — OPTIONS blocks it first Yes

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Every decision node runs inside the browser. A blocked response was often still delivered and still executed server-side — the browser merely refused to hand it to script, which is why a "blocked by CORS" error can sit alongside a 200 in your access log.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't use CORS as an authorization mechanism. It restricts what browser JavaScript may read, nothing more. A curl call, a mobile app or a scraper never consults it. Authorization belongs in tokens, sessions and network policy.

Don't reach for CORS when a same-origin path exists. Serving the API under /api on the same origin, via a reverse proxy or a path-based route, removes every preflight and every credential edge case. One proxy rule beats a permanent header matrix.

Don't preflight on hot paths without checking Access-Control-Max-Age. An uncached preflight doubles the round trips on every call. If your chattiest endpoint sends application/json with a custom header, that's a measurable P95 tax.

Don't reflect the Origin header without an allowlist. Reflection plus Allow-Credentials: true is functionally equivalent to disabling the same-origin policy for anyone who can get a victim to load their page.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A CORS error means the request never reached my server."

✅ Reality: For a simple request it usually did reach the server and ran to completion, side effects included. The browser blocked only the response from reaching JavaScript. Preflighted requests are the exception: a rejected OPTIONS does stop the real request from being sent.

❌ Misconception: "CORS protects my API from other sites."

✅ Reality: The same-origin policy is the protection; CORS is the mechanism for selectively relaxing it. A permissive CORS policy weakens a browser-side default and has zero effect on any non-browser caller. Treating it as a security control leaves the real gate unbuilt.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — the safe-method set is what the simple-request rule is built on.

  • Cookies and cookie attributes (Item 63) — credentialed CORS only makes sense once SameSite is understood.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • HTTP caching (Item 62) — Vary: Origin is a caching problem wearing a CORS costume. Read immediately after this.

  • Choosing the right status code (Item 60) — a preflight that returns 401 or 405 fails opaquely in the console.

  • Rate limiting (Item 69) — preflights count as requests and can consume quota twice per call.

notes.title: Content Negotiation and Compression
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Negotiation mechanics — MDN: Content negotiation

  • Normative header definitions — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Three negotiation headers? Accept (media type) · Accept-Encoding (compression) · Accept-Language.
Mandatory response header when compressing? Vary: Accept-Encoding. Omit it and shared caches serve undecodable bodies.
When is compression a waste? JPEG, MP4, zip — already compressed, so you burn CPU for ~0%.

Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Server-driven content negotiation is the client stating preferences on the request — Accept, Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language, each with optional q-values — and the server picking one representation and declaring what it picked. Compression is the negotiation that actually moves numbers: gzip is universal, brotli typically produces smaller text than gzip at comparable cost and is the right default for static assets, and zstd hits similar ratios at noticeably higher speed, which matters for dynamic responses compressed per request. The rule that bites people is Vary: Accept-Encoding. Without it, a CDN or reverse proxy caches one encoding and hands a brotli body to a client that only advertised gzip — the client sees binary garbage, and it reproduces only for the users behind that cache node. The second rule is to skip compression entirely on already-compressed formats: JPEG, PNG, MP4 and zip gain nothing, so you pay CPU and latency for a rounding error.

Where it matters: CDN configuration, API gateway defaults, and every "corrupt response for some users only" bug — which is a missing Vary until proven otherwise. (→ Item 62)

notes.title: Range Requests and Resumable Downloads
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Range mechanics end to end — MDN: HTTP range requests

  • 206 and 416 definitions — MDN: HTTP response status codes

🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Server advertises support how? Accept-Ranges: bytes on the full response. none means unsupported.
Success and failure codes? 206 Partial Content with Content-Range; 416 when the range is unsatisfiable.
What makes a resume safe? If-Range with the ETag — a changed file returns the whole 200 instead.

Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Range requests let a client ask for bytes rather than documents. The server advertises Accept-Ranges: bytes, the client sends Range: bytes=0-1023, and the server answers 206 Partial Content with a Content-Range naming the served span and the total size. An out-of-bounds range returns 416 Range Not Satisfiable. The header that makes this trustworthy is If-Range: pass the ETag you originally received, and if the resource has changed the server ignores the range and sends the full 200 rather than stitching two versions of a file into one corrupt artifact. That's the difference between a resume and silent data corruption, and it's why validators and ranges are one topic, not two. (→ Item 61)

Where it matters: resumable large-file downloads such as model weights and installers, video seeking without fetching the whole file, and parallel chunked transfer that opens several connections at different offsets. The failure mode worth remembering: an intermediary proxy that strips Accept-Ranges silently disables all three, and downloads restart from zero with no error anywhere in the logs.

notes.title: Idempotency Keys

headings.text: Walk me through exactly what the server does when a request with an Idempotency-Key arrives.
The operation fails halfway through. Do you release the key, or record the failure?
You've put a dedup store in front of every write. What breaks at scale, and what do you do when it's down?
Design idempotency for an LLM completion endpoint billed per token.
🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The reference implementation — Stripe: Idempotent requests

  • Method properties this works around — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, §9.2

  • Why POST needs it and PUT doesn't — MDN: HTTP request methods

  • The retry behaviour it must survive — AWS: Exponential Backoff And Jitter

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
One key per what? Per logical operation — reused across every retry of it, never per attempt.
Why is "check, then process" broken? Two concurrent retries both find nothing, both charge.
What does the stored record hold? Key, state, request fingerprint, response status and body, expiry.
Same key, different body? Reject. Never silently replay an answer to a different request.
How long a TTL? Longer than the client's whole retry window. Stripe keeps 24 hours.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Day before interview — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

POST carries no idempotency guarantee, so a timeout leaves the client unable to tell whether the charge happened. An idempotency key buys the guarantee back: the client generates a UUID once per logical operation and sends it on every retry. The server's first action, before any side effect, is an atomic insert of that key under a uniqueness constraint. The winner does the work and stores its response; a loser replays it. The design lives or dies on that insert being atomic rather than a check-then-act.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through exactly what the server does when a request with an Idempotency-Key arrives.

🎯 Really testing: whether you place the insert before the side effect, and what you store.

Before touching the payment processor, the queue or anything else, the server inserts the key into a dedup table under a uniqueness constraint, in state processing. If the insert succeeds, this request owns the operation and may proceed; if the constraint rejects it, an earlier attempt owns it and this request must not do the work.

The record holds five things: the key, the state (processing or complete), a fingerprint hashed from the canonicalised request body, the response status and body once known, and an expiry. Storing the response is what lets a replay return the original 201 with the original charge ID rather than a bare acknowledgement.

Scoping matters more than people expect: per endpoint and per API key or tenant. Without tenant scoping, one customer sends another's key and gets their response body — a cross-tenant leak dressed as a cache hit. Without endpoint scoping, a key reused across /charges and /refunds collides on a shared namespace.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

The operation fails halfway through. Do you release the key, or record the failure?

📍 Seen in the wild: the bug that shows as "the customer retried and got the same error forever".

Two defensible designs; the choice is which failure you would rather explain.

Release the key — delete the processing row so a retry genuinely re-attempts. Right when the failure is transient and provably preceded the side effect: a connection reset before the charge was submitted. The risk is that "never reached a side effect" is usually unverifiable. If the processor did receive it and you released the key, the retry charges twice — the exact problem the key existed to solve.

Record the failure as the outcome — mark the record complete with the 5xx stored, and replay it. Right when you cannot prove the side effect did not happen. Safe, and frustrating: the client is locked into the failure for the whole TTL and must mint a new key, a real cost when the failure was transient.

My default: record the failure whenever the side effect is money or externally visible, and release only for failures that provably precede the first external call — validation, auth, quota.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

You've put a dedup store in front of every write. What breaks at scale, and what do you do when it's down?

🎯 Really testing: whether you notice you have added a hard dependency to the write path.

The store takes full write QPS with two round trips per request — the insert, then the completion update — both on the critical path before any work begins. A few milliseconds on every write to save the rare duplicate is usually worth it, but the store's p99 is now a floor under your API's. It also needs a TTL sweep: at 10k writes/sec with a 24-hour TTL you hold roughly 864M live rows, so expiry must be a partitioned drop or a native TTL, never a DELETE WHERE expires_at < now() scan.

Availability is the harder question. The write path's availability is now the product of the service's and the store's, so a store at 99.9% caps a 99.99% service. Co-locate it, replicate it, treat it as tier-0.

When it is down you pick a failure mode, and it differs by workload. Payments: fail closed — reject with 503 and Retry-After. A brief outage is recoverable; a duplicate charge is a chargeback and a regulatory smell. LLM inference: fail open — process without dedup, since a duplicate generation costs tokens and is cheaper than refusing all traffic. The trade is one duplicate's cost against the whole endpoint's availability.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design idempotency for an LLM completion endpoint billed per token.

🎯 Really testing: whether you notice the stored response is now large, and that regenerating is the thing you must prevent.

The mechanism is unchanged — client UUID per logical operation, atomic insert under a uniqueness constraint, fingerprint over the canonicalised request. What changes is the replay. For a payment it returns a small JSON receipt; here it must return the stored completion byte for byte, because regeneration is both the expensive step and a non-deterministic one — the same prompt at temperature 0.7 gives a different answer. Regenerating breaks the contract, not just the budget.

So the record splits. Metadata — key, state, fingerprint, status, token counts, expiry — stays in the transactional store where the uniqueness constraint lives. The completion body goes to object storage behind a pointer: a 100KB response times 864M rows does not belong in the same database as your concurrency primitive. Streaming complicates it — I would buffer and store the full text on completion, and replay that, rather than pretend to replay a stream.

The fingerprint needs care here. Canonicalise model, prompt, temperature, seed and max tokens; exclude request IDs and timestamps, or every retry looks like a different request and the key never matches.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Approach Who owns identity Needs a store Choose it when
PUT /orders/{client-uuid} Client No The client can own the ID — simplest possible retry safety
Natural unique key + DB constraint The domain No (reuses your table) The operation already has real identity: invoice no., delivery ID
Idempotency-Key header Client, for dedup only Yes You need server-generated IDs and POST semantics
Client-side reconciliation (GET before retry) Nobody No Legacy server you cannot change — racy, last resort
No dedup — No Side effects are cheap and reversible, e.g. an idempotent cache warm

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Nail the ticket to the peg before you take the coat.

You write a number on a cloakroom ticket before handing over your coat, and keep that number all night. The attendant nails the ticket to a peg first — one ticket per peg, physically — and only then hangs the coat. If a second person rushes the counter with the same number, the peg is taken: they wait until the coat is hanging, then get that coat back, not a second one. At closing time every unclaimed peg is cleared.

Story beat Mechanism
Writing the number before handing over the coat Client generates the key per logical operation, before the first attempt
Nailing the ticket to the peg first Atomic insert under a uniqueness constraint, before any side effect
Peg tagged but no coat on it yet processing state — winner is mid-flight
Second person waits at the counter Loser polls, or gets 409 and retries into the replay
Coat on the peg, handed back complete state with the stored response replayed
Attendant checks the coat matches the description Request fingerprint — same key, different body is rejected
Closing time clears the racks TTL, which must outlast the client's retry window

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No math — the mechanism is a concurrency protocol whose entire correctness rests on one atomic write happening before one side effect.

  BROKEN — check then act              CORRECT — the insert IS the lock
  ───────────────────────              ────────────────────────────────
  A: SELECT key -> not found           A: INSERT key -> wins  (owns it)
  B: SELECT key -> not found           B: INSERT key -> conflict (loses)
  A: charge  $49.99                    A: charge $49.99, store 201
  B: charge  $49.99   <-- DUPLICATE    B: reads A's row -> replays 201

  The window between B's SELECT and A's INSERT is where the money goes.
  It is microseconds wide and a retry storm hits it constantly.

  Record: (tenant, endpoint, key) UNIQUE | state | fingerprint | status | body | expires_at

The uniqueness constraint is the concurrency primitive, not a validation. Anything that reads first and writes second — an application-level exists() check, a cache lookup, a Redis GET before SET — reintroduces the race no matter how small the window looks.

7. Why It Matters in Production

A timeout on a write is ambiguous by construction, and no client-side cleverness resolves it. Idempotency keys make the ambiguity harmless instead of resolving it — which is why every payments API converged on the same header. (→ Item 58)

The failure mode is quiet. Duplicate charges throw no exceptions; they surface days later as chargebacks, by which point the request logs have rotated. Build one detection signal up front: the rate of key conflicts whose fingerprint mismatches. That means clients are reusing keys across different operations, and it ends with one customer receiving another's response.

8. Code / Pseudocode Example

The atomic insert plus the three branches. This is the example traced in Section 9.

# ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes the INSERT itself the lock. A SELECT-then-INSERT
# leaves a window where two concurrent retries both proceed and both charge.
INS = """INSERT INTO idem (tenant, endpoint, key, fingerprint, state, expires_at)
         VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, 'processing', now() + interval '24 hours')
         ON CONFLICT (tenant, endpoint, key) DO NOTHING RETURNING id"""

def handle(cur, tenant, key, body):
    fp = sha256(canonical_json(body))       # excludes timestamps / request ids
    cur.execute(INS, (tenant, "/v1/charges", key, fp))
    if cur.fetchone():                      # BRANCH 1 — we won: do the work
        resp = charge(body)                 # the ONLY place the side effect happens
        cur.execute("UPDATE idem SET state='complete', status=201, body=%s "
                    "WHERE tenant=%s AND endpoint=%s AND key=%s",
                    (json.dumps(resp), tenant, "/v1/charges", key))
        return 201, resp
    row = fetch(cur, tenant, "/v1/charges", key)
    if row.fingerprint != fp:               # same key, different request — never replay
        return 422, {"error": "idempotency_key_reused_with_different_body"}
    if row.state == "complete":             # BRANCH 2 — replay the stored response
        return row.status, json.loads(row.body)
    return 409, {"error": "request_in_progress"}   # BRANCH 3 — winner still running

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

One logical charge, tenant=acct_42, key=idem_7a1e, body {"amount": 4999, "currency": "usd"}, fingerprint sha256 = b91c…. The client's first attempt times out at 10s, so it retries — while the first attempt is still running.

  t=0.00s  ATTEMPT 1 ─ INSERT (acct_42, /v1/charges, idem_7a1e, b91c…, processing)
           ✅ returned a row  ── WE WON ── calling the processor…
  t=0.01s  🗄️  idem: idem_7a1e | processing | b91c… | null | null

  t=10.0s  client times out (response still in flight) and retries the SAME key
           ATTEMPT 2 ─ INSERT same tuple
           ❌ ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING → no row  ── WE LOST
           reads row: fingerprint b91c… matches ✅, state = processing
           ⚠️ 409 request_in_progress   (no second charge)

  t=11.4s  ATTEMPT 1 returns ch_9f2c → UPDATE state=complete, status=201
           🗄️  idem: idem_7a1e | complete | b91c… | 201 | {"id":"ch_9f2c",…}

  t=12.0s  ATTEMPT 3 (client backed off, same key) ─ INSERT → conflict
           fingerprint matches ✅, state = complete
           ✅ 201 {"id":"ch_9f2c"}  ── REPLAYED, one charge on the card

  t=12.5s  a buggy client sends idem_7a1e with {"amount": 9999}
           fingerprint 4de0… ≠ b91c…  →  ❌ 422, and an alert fires

  1. Attempt 2 is stopped by the constraint, not by a check. No application code compared anything — the database rejected the second insert. That is why the microsecond-wide race in the SELECT-first version cannot occur.

  2. 409 rather than blocking is deliberate. The loser could poll for the winner's result; 409 pushes the wait onto the client's existing backoff and keeps a server thread free. Under a retry storm that is the whole capacity argument. (→ Item 68)

  3. The replay at t=12.0s returns ch_9f2c, not a bare 200. The client needs the charge ID it never received. Storing only "already done" would leave it with no way to reconcile.

  4. The 422 at t=12.5s is the signal worth alerting on. A fingerprint mismatch means a client is reusing keys across different operations; left alone, that eventually returns one customer's response to another.

10. When TO Use This

Use it when the side effect is expensive or irreversible and the client must retry — payments, refunds, provisioning, outbound email, billed LLM generation.

Use it when you need server-generated identifiers — the whole reason to prefer this over PUT /orders/{client-uuid}, which is simpler but surrenders ID assignment. (→ Item 58)

Use it on any endpoint an SDK or gateway retries automatically. If a layer in your path retries POSTs, keys are the only thing between you and duplicate writes.

Use it for webhook receivers too — the delivery ID a provider stamps on each event is an idempotency key you did not have to design.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't add it when a natural unique key exists. An invoice number or delivery ID with a uniqueness constraint on your existing table gives the same guarantee with no parallel store, TTL or sweep job.

Don't add it to reads or already-idempotent writes. A GET, or a PUT to a client-chosen URI, gets the property free from the method. The store is pure overhead.

Don't generate the key per attempt. A client minting a fresh UUID inside its retry loop has an ordinary non-idempotent POST wearing a header — the most common bug in the pattern, invisible until a duplicate lands.

Don't rely on it for ordering. Keys make a duplicate harmless; they say nothing about two different updates arriving out of order. That needs If-Match. (→ Item 61)

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Idempotency keys give you exactly-once delivery."

✅ Reality: Delivery stays at-least-once — you cannot prevent duplicate arrivals over an unreliable network. The key gives you idempotent processing, so duplicate arrivals produce exactly-once effects. Not pedantry: it tells you where the mechanism lives (the server's write path, not the transport) and why the store must be as durable as the operation it protects.

❌ Misconception: "Redis with SETNX and a TTL is enough."

✅ Reality: SETNX is genuinely atomic, so the race is handled — but Redis is not in the same transaction as your business write. If the key is set and the process dies before the charge commits, you have a key claiming an operation that never happened, and the retry replays a result that does not exist. Put the key in the same transactional store as the side effect, or budget for a reconciliation job.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning):

❌ I thought the point of the key was to let the server recognise a repeat, so I wrote if store.exists(key): return cached and moved on.

✅ Recognition is the easy half. The hard half is that recognition must be the mutual exclusion — the insert wins or loses atomically, before any side effect. My version left a window between check and write that a retry storm hits reliably, and it charged twice under exactly the conditions the key was added to survive.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Describing "check if the key exists, then process". This is the single answer interviewers listen for. The insert must be the concurrency primitive; anything read-then-write races.

Not saying what is stored. "I store the key" is half a design. Without the response status and body you cannot replay a useful answer; without the fingerprint you replay the wrong one.

Skipping the scope. Scope keys per tenant and per endpoint, or a client probes another tenant's keys and reads their responses. Say it unprompted.

Ignoring the TTL/retry-window relationship. A TTL shorter than the client's retry window means a late retry finds no record and re-executes — the duplicate you built all this to prevent, hours late.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Stripe key retention 24 hours Results are replayed within the window, then the key is free Stripe API docs
Stripe key reuse with different params Returns an error Never silently replays the wrong response Stripe API docs
Recommended key format V4 UUID 122 random bits — collision risk negligible across tenants Stripe API docs
Live rows at 10k writes/s, 24h TTL ~864M Why expiry must be partition-drop or native TTL, not a DELETE scan Derived (10,000 × 86,400)
Extra round trips per write 2 Insert before work, update after — both on the critical path This design
Dedup store availability Multiplies with the service's 99.9% store caps a 99.99% service Derived
Fingerprint size 32 bytes (SHA-256) Cheap to store per row, cheap to compare SHA-256 output length

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Two extra store round trips per write, both on the critical path before any work starts. Single-digit ms same-AZ — verify against your own store's p99, since it becomes a floor under your API's.
💰 Cost Pure overhead in the happy path. Pays for itself the first time it stops one duplicate charge or one duplicate 50k-token generation.
🎯 Quality Turns a timeout from a customer-visible incident into a retry. The largest single lever on write-path reliability once the network is unreliable.
📈 Scale The store takes full write QPS, holds hundreds of millions of live rows at a 24-hour TTL, and needs partitioned expiry. It is a real system, not a table.
🔧 Ops Complexity A tier-0 dependency, a TTL sweep, a fail-open/fail-closed decision, a fingerprint-mismatch path, and a failure-release policy. Compare: PUT /{uuid} costs none of these.

16. Real World Usage

Stripe defined the convention — Idempotency-Key on POST, results saved for 24 hours, an error rather than a replay when the same key arrives with different parameters. Most payments and billing APIs copied the header name and the semantics.

AWS exposes the same idea as ClientToken on EC2 RunInstances and similar create calls, which is why a retried launch does not give you two instances. The vocabulary differs; the constraint underneath does not.

Kafka's idempotent producer generalises it past HTTP: a producer ID plus a per-partition sequence number lets the broker discard duplicate sends — the same "identity supplied by the caller, deduplicated at the destination" shape, with the key folded into the protocol rather than a header.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — why POST needs this and PUT does not. Read first.

  • HTTP methods & their contracts (Item 57) — the contracts this restores for POST.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • Timeouts, retries & backoff (Item 68) — the client behaviour the TTL and 409 branch must survive.

  • Status codes (Item 59) — 409 for in-progress, 422 for fingerprint mismatch, 503 when the store is down.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • PUT /resource/{client-uuid} — no store, no TTL, no race; costs server-generated IDs.

  • Natural unique key on the domain table — reuses a constraint you have; only when the operation has real-world identity.

  • Reconcile-before-retry on the client — racy and adds an unhappy-path round trip; only for servers you cannot change.

  • Distributed lock plus a result cache — strictly worse: two systems to keep consistent where one constraint suffices.

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • ETags and If-Match (Item 61) — preconditions handle ordering, which keys do not.

  • Rate limiting (Item 69) — a 429 is a retryable failure, so it must retry into the same key.

  • L4 vs L7 load balancing (Item 4) — the proxy's retry-on-POST setting is safe only because these keys exist.

19. System Design Application

Place the dedup store deliberately: behind the API service and inside the same transactional boundary as the side effect wherever possible. One Postgres table alongside the charges table beats a separate Redis cluster, because the key row and the business row commit or roll back together. The moment they are separate systems, you owe a reconciliation job for crashes between the two writes.

Shard by the key itself: every lookup is an exact match on (tenant, endpoint, key), so no range scans and no cross-shard joins. The break-points are storage and expiry, not query complexity — 864M live rows at 10k writes/sec forces time-partitioned tables you drop wholesale rather than delete row by row.

Monitor four series, not one:

Signal Why Act when
Insert conflict rate Normal retry level Sudden rise means a retry storm upstream
Conflicts with fingerprint mismatch Clients reusing keys across operations Any sustained rate — this leaks responses
409 processing rate Concurrent retries arriving mid-flight Rising = client timeout is below server p99
Store p99 and error rate It is a floor under your write latency Approaching your latency budget

For SLOs, the endpoint's availability is the product of the service's and the store's, so the store needs a stricter target than the API it protects — 99.99% behind a 99.9% API, not the reverse. Budget the latency explicitly: at a 300ms p99 target, an 8ms store costs 2.7% of the budget before any work starts. Quote that number when someone proposes putting the store in another region.

A downstream dependency degrades to 5-second latency. Trace what happens without protection, then add safeguards in order of leverage.
