🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)
How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion
Where this typically breaks at scale, and what to alert on

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Jitter strategies, with simulation results — Exponential Backoff And Jitter (AWS Architecture Blog)

  • Retry-After semantics — MDN: Retry-After header

  • Which codes are retryable — MDN: HTTP response status codes

  • Method properties (normative) — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The Full Jitter formula? sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)) — randomise the whole interval.
Why jitter at all? Without it, every retrying client wakes simultaneously and re-synchronises the herd.
Retry amplification, 3 layers × 3 attempts? 27× worst case. Retry at one layer, not every layer.
Which codes do you retry? 408, 429, 502, 503, 504, connect errors, timeouts. Never 400/401/403/404/422.
What must timeouts do down a call chain? Shrink. A caller's budget must exceed the sum of everything below it.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Day before interview — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Retries turn transient failures into invisible ones, and under load they turn a slow dependency into an outage. The client-side contract has four parts: a timeout that's actually shorter than your caller's, retries scoped to failures that could plausibly succeed later, exponential backoff so you don't hammer a struggling service, and jitter so ten thousand clients don't all wake at the same millisecond. The part people skip is the budget — capping retries as a fraction of successful traffic, so amplification stays constant instead of compounding per layer.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through the four jitter strategies and which one you'd pick.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name a specific formula, or only gesture at "add some randomness".

Plain exponential backoff is sleep = min(cap, base × 2^attempt) — deterministic, and that determinism is the bug. Every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment, so retry traffic arrives as a spike and the dependency you're trying to let recover gets a synchronised wave.

The three jittered variants differ in how much of the interval they randomise. Full Jitter takes random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)) — the entire window. Equal Jitter keeps half deterministic: temp/2 + random(0, temp/2). Decorrelated Jitter walks from the previous sleep: min(cap, random(base, prev × 3)).

I'd pick Full Jitter, and cite the reason rather than assert it: AWS's simulation found it reduced both total server work and total completion time, and Equal Jitter's extra determinism bought nothing. It's also the simplest to implement correctly, which matters when this code gets copied into every service you own.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

How do you set timeouts across a chain of three services?

📍 Seen in the wild: common follow-on to any latency question; often phrased as "why did the whole chain hang".

🎯 Really testing: whether you think in budgets that propagate, or set each service's timeout independently.

Timeouts must shrink going down the chain, and the way to guarantee it is to propagate a deadline rather than configure a duration per hop. If the edge grants 3 seconds, service A passes "you have 2.8s left" to B, and B passes the remainder to C. gRPC deadlines and Go's context.WithTimeout do this natively; over plain HTTP you carry the remaining budget in a header.

The failure when you don't is common and specific: each service independently configured with a 30-second timeout means a slow C holds B, which holds A, which holds the edge — every pool occupied for 30 seconds while the user gave up at 3. The tier then falls over from resource exhaustion rather than from the original slowness.

Concretely: separate connect and read timeouts, connect kept short since a healthy handshake is one RTT, read set from the propagated remainder. The check that catches a misconfiguration is each hop's P99 against the timeout above it — if any hop's timeout exceeds its caller's remaining budget, the config is wrong regardless of how the dashboards look today.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

A downstream dependency degrades to 5-second latency. Trace what happens without protection, then add safeguards in order of leverage.

📍 Seen in the wild: a standard architect probe; it's the anatomy of most cascading-failure postmortems.

Without protection it propagates upward as resource exhaustion, not as errors. Callers block on the slow dependency, each holding a connection and a thread; the pool saturates; requests that never touch that dependency queue behind ones that do. Then retries fire — it's slow, not down, so requests time out and get retried, multiplying load on something already struggling. That's a metastable failure: the retry backlog keeps the system down even after the original slowness clears, so it doesn't recover when you'd expect.

In order of leverage: first a timeout shorter than the caller's budget, because nothing else can engage without it — you cannot shed load you're still waiting on. Second, bulkheading with a separate pool per dependency, so saturating the slow one leaves the rest functional. Third, the circuit breaker, which stops calls once the failure rate crosses a threshold and lets the dependency recover instead of being held down. Fourth, the retry budget.

The signal I'd instrument first is in-flight requests per dependency, alerting well before pool exhaustion. Error rate lags — by the time it spikes the pool is full and the cascade has started.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the resilience layer for a service calling an LLM provider with P99 latency of 20 seconds and occasional 429s.

🎯 Really testing: whether you notice that long, expensive, streaming calls break the usual retry assumptions.

A retry here is expensive in both money and time — reissuing a 20-second generation costs a second full generation — so "retry three times and move on" is wrong. I'd separate the failure classes first. A 429 with Retry-After isn't a failure but a schedule: honour the header rather than applying my own backoff, since the provider knows its capacity. A connection error before any tokens arrive is cheap to retry. A failure mid-stream, after tokens were delivered, isn't retryable at all without duplicating billed output.

That last case drives the design. Every request carries an idempotency key so a retry the provider already processed returns the stored completion rather than regenerating (→ Item 67). A P99 of 20 seconds means a large per-attempt timeout and a larger total budget, so the user-facing contract must be streaming or async with a polling URL — no synchronous 60-second request survives a real proxy chain (→ Item 4).

For provider failure I'd use a per-provider circuit breaker with fallback to a second provider rather than retrying the first harder, capped by a budget at ~10% of successful calls. The signal I'd watch is cost per successful completion, not error rate — a retry storm against an LLM provider hits the invoice days before anyone reads it off a latency graph.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Strategy Formula Behaviour
No backoff sleep = 0 Hammers a struggling service. Never correct.
Fixed delay sleep = base No spike relief; all clients still synchronised.
Exponential, no jitter min(cap, base × 2^n) Spreads over time, but clients stay synchronised.
Full Jitter ✅ random(0, min(cap, base × 2^n)) Best on total work and completion time in AWS's simulation.
Equal Jitter t/2 + random(0, t/2) where t = min(cap, base × 2^n) Half deterministic; extra complexity, no measured gain.
Decorrelated Jitter min(cap, random(base, prev × 3)) Walks upward from the last sleep; competitive, more state.

Retryable vs not:

Retry Don't retry
Connect errors, timeouts, connection resets 400 Bad Request, 422 Unprocessable Content
408 Request Timeout, 429 Too Many Requests 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden
502, 503, 504 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed
— (only if idempotent or key-carrying) 501 Not Implemented

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Everyone redials at once.

The phone line to the box office is engaged. Five hundred people hang up and hit redial after exactly ten seconds — so at second ten the switchboard takes five hundred simultaneous calls and jams again. Now they all wait twenty, then forty, still in lockstep, and the switchboard is idle between waves and drowning during them. The fix isn't waiting longer; it's each person rolling a die to decide how long to wait, so the same five hundred calls arrive spread across the interval instead of stacked at one instant.

Story beat Mechanism
Line engaged Dependency saturated or failing
Everyone redials at ten seconds Deterministic backoff, clients synchronised
Doubling to twenty, then forty Exponential backoff without jitter
Idle between waves, drowning during them The spike pattern that keeps a service from recovering
Rolling a die for how long to wait Full Jitter — randomise the whole interval
Giving up after a few tries Retry cap plus circuit breaker

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

No math beyond one formula — the mechanism is a decision procedure plus a randomised delay.

Why determinism is the enemy, in one picture — 500 clients failing at t=0, base 1s:

NO JITTER — clients stay in lockstep, server sees spikes and idles
  t=1s   ████████████████████████ 500 requests   ← jams again
  t=3s   ████████████████████████ 500 requests   ← jams again
  t=7s   ████████████████████████ 500 requests
         (nothing at all in between)

FULL JITTER — random(0, min(cap, base × 2^n)) spreads the same load
  t=0-1s ███ ██ ███ ██ ███ ██ ███  ~500 spread across the window
  t=1-3s ██ ███ ██ ███ ██ ███ ██
  t=3-7s ███ ██ ███ ██ ███
         same total requests, no instant exceeds capacity

RETRY AMPLIFICATION — why the budget matters more than the backoff
  browser 3× → gateway 3× → service 3×  =  3³ = 27 backend calls
  per single user request, in the worst case

The budget is the part people omit, and it's the one that bounds the blast radius. Backoff spreads retries over time; a budget caps their total volume. Implemented as a token bucket refilled by successful requests, it turns amplification from a power of the layer count into a constant — typically 10–20% above baseline no matter how many layers exist.

7. Why It Matters in Production

Retries are the highest-leverage lever on user-visible error rate, because most distributed failures are transient — a rebalancing partition, a pod terminating, one dropped packet. A correct policy makes those invisible.

The same mechanism is the most common way a partial degradation becomes a full outage. Retries are cheap when everything is healthy and expensive exactly when it isn't, so a policy that looked harmless in testing becomes a load multiplier at the worst moment. Retry storms are a positive feedback loop producing metastable failures — systems that stay down after the triggering fault is fixed, because the backlog sustains the overload.

8. Code / Pseudocode Example

Full Jitter with a retry budget and Retry-After honoured. Traced in Section 9.

import random, time, httpx

RETRYABLE = {408, 429, 502, 503, 504}
BASE, CAP, MAX_ATTEMPTS = 0.5, 20.0, 4      # seconds; cap stops unbounded growth

def call(client, req, key, budget):
    for n in range(MAX_ATTEMPTS):
        try:
            r = client.send(req, headers={"Idempotency-Key": key})   # SAME key every attempt
            if r.status_code not in RETRYABLE:
                budget.record_success()
                return r                                              # incl. 4xx — do not retry those
            wait = float(r.headers.get("Retry-After", 0)) or None     # provider knows its own capacity
        except (httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ReadTimeout):
            wait = None                                               # no response, so no hint
        if n == MAX_ATTEMPTS - 1 or not budget.allow():
            break                                                     # budget exhausted: shed, don't pile on
        # Full Jitter: randomise the WHOLE interval, not just a fraction of it
        time.sleep(wait if wait is not None else random.uniform(0, min(CAP, BASE * 2 ** n)))
    raise RuntimeError("exhausted retries")

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Same code. 500 clients hit a backend that starts returning 503, recovering at t≈4s. BASE=0.5, CAP=20, budget = 10% of successes.

📥 t=0.0s   500 clients → 503 Service Unavailable (no Retry-After)
    │
    ▼
🎲 [1] each client: sleep = random(0, min(20, 0.5 × 2⁰)) = random(0, 0.5)
    │        → 500 retries spread across 0.0–0.5s, not stacked at 0.5s
    ▼
📥 t≈0.3s   still 503. Budget check: retries so far ≈ 500, successes ≈ 0
    │
    ▼
🛑 [2] budget.allow() → False for most clients — 10% cap already breached
    │        → they FAIL FAST instead of amplifying. This is the load shed.
    ▼
🎲 [3] the ~50 clients still in budget: sleep = random(0, min(20, 0.5×2¹)) = random(0, 1.0)
    │
    ▼
✅ t≈4.2s   backend recovers. The ~50 in-budget clients succeed,
    │        refilling the budget, which re-admits the rest gradually
    ▼
🎯 Result: backend saw ~550 requests during the outage, not 500 × 4 = 2000

  1. Jitter did its job in step 1 — the same 500 retries arrived spread across a window instead of as one spike. Without it the backend takes 500 simultaneous requests at exactly t=0.5s and stays jammed.

  2. The budget did the more important job in step 2. Backoff alone still produces 2,000 total requests, just spread out. The budget cut that to ~550 by refusing retries past 10% of successes — and it refuses them without waiting, so those clients fail fast and release their connections.

  3. Recovery is gradual by construction. The budget refills from successes, so a recovering backend re-admits retry traffic in proportion to what it can serve. Without a budget the full backlog lands at once and can re-break it — the classic failed recovery.

  4. Retry-After overrides the computed sleep whenever present. On a 429 the provider is stating its actual capacity window; a local exponential guess is strictly worse information.

10. When TO Use This

Use it on every call crossing a process boundary. Most HTTP clients default to either no retries or naive ones, and both are wrong for production.

Use a retry budget wherever more than one layer can retry — nearly every microservice architecture. It's the difference between bounded and compounding amplification.

Use Retry-After over your own backoff whenever the server sends it: on 429 and 503 it's stating its actual recovery window, which beats any client-side guess.

Use deadline propagation rather than per-hop timeouts on any chain deeper than two services, so the budget genuinely shrinks instead of nominally doing so.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't retry non-idempotent operations without an idempotency key. A retried POST /payments charges twice. (→ Items 58, 67)

Don't retry deterministic failures. A 400 or 422 fails identically forever; retrying wastes the budget a genuinely transient failure needed, and across a large fleet it's an accidental self-DDoS against a permanently-failing endpoint.

Don't retry at more than one layer. Pick the layer with the most context — usually the service client, which knows whether the operation is idempotent — and make every other layer fail fast. Browser plus gateway plus service is how 3 becomes 27.

Don't retry an expensive operation like a cheap one. A retried 20-second generation costs a full second generation in latency and money; the right move there is a fallback provider or a degraded response.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Exponential backoff is enough — jitter is a micro-optimisation."

✅ Reality: Backoff without jitter keeps clients synchronised, so the server sees spikes separated by idle gaps rather than smooth load. AWS's simulation found Full Jitter cut both total server work and total completion time versus plain exponential backoff. Jitter is the part that lets the dependency recover.

❌ Misconception: "More retries means higher availability."

✅ Reality: More retries raise availability while failures are rare and independent, and lower it during a correlated failure — which is when availability actually matters. Past a point they're indistinguishable from a denial-of-service attack you're running against yourself, which is why the budget matters more than the attempt count.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning):

❌ I treated timeouts as a per-service setting — pick a sensible number for each service and move on.

✅ Timeouts are a budget that propagates, not a local setting. Thirty seconds set independently at three hops means the top of the chain waits 30 seconds for work the user abandoned at 3, with every pool along the way full of requests nobody awaits. Once I propagated a deadline instead of configuring durations, a whole category of cascading-failure incidents stopped happening.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Describing backoff without mentioning jitter. The most common gap, and the part that determines whether the dependency can recover. Naming Full Jitter with its formula is a concrete, checkable signal.

Not distinguishing retryable from non-retryable failures. "Retry on error" is a junior answer; the senior version names the classes and the test — could this same request plausibly succeed later?

Talking about retries without amplification. Anyone can add a retry loop. The architect content is the budget, the single-layer rule, and the 3³ arithmetic motivating both.

Forgetting the circuit breaker. Retries handle transient failures, breakers handle sustained ones. A retry-only policy keeps hammering a dependency that's been down ten minutes — exactly the traffic preventing recovery.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Full Jitter formula random(0, min(cap, base × 2^n)) Best on total work and completion time in AWS's simulation AWS Architecture Blog, Exponential Backoff And Jitter
Retry amplification, 3 layers × 3 attempts 27× Why retries belong at exactly one layer Derived (3³)
Typical retry budget 10–20% of successful requests Bounds amplification to a constant Common practice — verify your mesh's default
Retryable status codes 408, 429, 502, 503, 504 Plus connect errors and timeouts RFC 9110 semantics; MDN status reference
Retry-After format Seconds, or an HTTP-date Sent on 429, 503, and some 3xx MDN Retry-After
Typical proxy idle timeout ~60 s Caps how long a synchronous retry chain can run Common default — verify yours (→ Item 4)

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Retries raise P99 by construction — a retried request costs its own latency plus the backoff. Improving success rate makes the tail worse; both are real, and the SLO has to say which you're optimising.
💰 Cost Every retry is a fully-billed request. Against a per-token LLM provider a retry storm shows up on the invoice before it shows up on a latency graph.
🎯 Quality The single largest lever on user-visible error rate, since most distributed failures are transient.
📈 Scale Amplification compounds per layer without a budget and stays constant with one. This is the difference between a degradation and an outage.
🔧 Ops Complexity Deadline propagation needs plumbing through every hop; budgets and breakers need per-dependency state and tuning. A mesh gives you all three as config, at the cost of running a mesh.

16. Real World Usage

AWS SDKs ship adaptive retry modes with jitter and a client-side rate limiter on by default — the strongest available evidence this is table stakes rather than an optimisation.

Envoy and gRPC expose retry_budget as first-class config precisely because amplification is well enough known to warrant a dedicated knob rather than an attempt count.

Stripe pairs retry guidance with Idempotency-Key — the two halves of this note together: the key makes a retry correct, the budget and backoff make it safe. (→ Item 67)

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • Safe vs idempotent vs cacheable (Item 58) — the property that decides whether retrying is legal at all.

  • Status codes (Item 59) and choosing the right code (Item 60) — the retryable/non-retryable split is a status-code decision.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next)

  • Idempotency keys (Item 67) — what makes a non-idempotent operation retryable.

  • Rate limiting (Item 69) — 429 plus Retry-After is the server half of this contract.

  • Timeouts & retries against LLM providers (Item 173) — this note applied to the AI serving path.

  • Triage playbooks (Item 167) — retry storms are a specific, recognisable incident shape.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Circuit breaker alone — choose it when failures are sustained rather than transient; complements retries, doesn't replace them.

  • Hedged requests — issue a second attempt after P95 rather than after failure. Choose it when latency matters more than load; reject it when the operation is expensive, since it roughly doubles cost.

  • Queue and process asynchronously — choose it when the caller doesn't need an answer now; converts a retry problem into a durability problem.

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Bulkheads / per-dependency connection pools — stop one slow dependency exhausting the whole service.

  • Deadline propagation (gRPC deadlines, context.WithTimeout) — the mechanism that makes timeouts actually shrink downward.

  • L4 vs L7 load balancing (Item 4) — the proxy has its own retry policy, and it counts as one of your layers.

19. System Design Application

Trigger gate: included. The retry policy is a component whose placement across hops, capacity implications and monitoring are the interview question, and it carries scale break-points the Tier 4 answer doesn't fully cover.

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

It arrives as "what happens when this dependency gets slow", and the weak answer is "we retry". The strong answer names where the retry lives, why one layer owns it, what bounds the volume, and what stops it entirely when the dependency is properly down. In AI-serving designs the probe sharpens to cost, because retrying a generation is expensive enough that the usual policy is wrong.

System context diagram

The non-obvious placement: the gateway sets the deadline but does not retry. Putting retries at the edge feels protective and is the fastest route to amplification, because the edge has the least context about whether an operation is idempotent.

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10x traffic Retry volume scales with failures, not requests — fine while failure rate is flat Budget already caps it; confirm the cap is on rate, not a fixed count
Correlated failure Every client retries at once; backend sees baseline × (1 + budget) Full Jitter to spread, budget to bound, breaker to stop
Recovery Backlog slams the recovering dependency and re-breaks it Budget refills from successes, so admission is gradual by construction
LLM tier A retry costs a full generation in latency and tokens Fallback provider over harder retries; idempotency key so a replay is free

Where this typically breaks at scale, and what to alert on

  • Retry amplification — alert on attempted-to-unique request ratio per hop. Near 1.0 steady-state; past ~1.2 the retry policy is part of the problem.

  • Pool exhaustion from missing timeouts — alert on in-flight requests per dependency. This leads error rate, which is a lagging indicator once the pool is already full.

  • Metastable failure — the system stays down after the trigger clears. The signal is retry rate staying high while the dependency's own latency has recovered.

  • Cost anomaly on paid dependencies — cost per successful completion, not total spend. A retry storm against an LLM provider is visible here days before anywhere else.

notes.title: Rate Limiting and 429

headings.text: Walk through the five common algorithms and what each one actually costs.
You're limiting to 100 req/min per key across 12 API nodes. Where do you keep the counter?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • 429 and neighbouring codes — MDN: HTTP response status codes

  • Telling the client when to come back — MDN: Retry-After

  • RateLimit fields — still an IETF Internet-Draft (v11), not an RFC — draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Token bucket vs leaky bucket in one line? Token bucket permits bursts to capacity; leaky bucket enforces constant outflow.
Fixed window's flaw? A 2× burst straddling the boundary — full quota twice in milliseconds.
429 vs 503? 429 = this client exceeded quota. 503 = server unavailable for everyone.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Rate limiting decides whether a request gets served or rejected based on how much that caller has already consumed. The algorithm choice is really a burst-tolerance choice: token bucket lets a client spend a saved-up burst up to capacity, leaky bucket refuses to and smooths output, fixed window is one counter per interval and permits double the limit across the boundary. The response contract matters as much as the algorithm — 429 plus Retry-After, so clients back off deterministically instead of hammering. Then the hard part starts: making the counter correct across many nodes.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk through the five common algorithms and what each one actually costs.

Token bucket holds a capacity and a refill rate: tokens accrue continuously, each request spends one, and a client idle for a while can burst up to capacity instantly. Leaky bucket is the dual — requests queue and drain at a fixed rate, so output is perfectly smooth and bursts are delayed rather than allowed. Fixed window keeps one counter per key per interval; it costs a single integer and one increment, but a client sending the full limit at 0:59 and again at 1:00 lands 2× the limit inside two seconds.

Sliding window log stores a timestamp per request and counts those inside the trailing interval — exact, and the reason it's rarely used is memory: 1000 requests per minute per client is 1000 timestamps held per client. Sliding window counter interpolates between the previous and current fixed windows weighted by elapsed time, which removes the boundary burst for two integers of state and small, bounded error. That last one is the default choice for most APIs, and token bucket is the default when bursts are legitimate.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

You're limiting to 100 req/min per key across 12 API nodes. Where do you keep the counter?

Per-node counters are free and wrong: 12 nodes each admitting 100 means an effective ceiling of 1200 req/min, and the error scales with your fleet, so an autoscaling event quietly raises everyone's limit. The dodge is dividing the limit by node count, which breaks the moment the load balancer isn't perfectly even or a node is draining. So the real choice is a shared store — Redis with an atomic Lua script implementing the token bucket — and the price is one network round trip on every request, typically 0.5–2 ms in-AZ, plus a new dependency in the request path.

The mitigation is a hybrid: keep an approximate local bucket per node, synchronise with Redis periodically or only as the client approaches its limit, and accept a small overshoot. Decide by what the limit is for. Abuse prevention and fairness tolerate 5–10% slop, so approximate is fine; billing quotas and hard downstream capacity limits do not, so pay the round trip. Fail open on Redis unavailability for fairness limits, fail closed for capacity protection — and alert either way, because a silently disabled limiter is how the next outage starts. (→ Item 60)

6. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (now - last_refill) × rate)
allow   = tokens ≥ 1        →  tokens -= 1
Retry-After = ceil((1 - tokens) / rate)   seconds

Advertise the outcome in headers: the IETF draft's RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy fields are the direction of travel but remain an Internet-Draft, so most clients still read the de-facto X-RateLimit-Limit, -Remaining and -Reset. Emit both, and always send Retry-After on the 429 itself.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Don't rate-limit as a substitute for capacity planning. A limiter that trips constantly under normal load is an outage with better error messages. If legitimate traffic hits the ceiling daily, the number is wrong or the service is undersized.

Don't key limits on IP alone. Corporate NATs, mobile carrier gateways and CI runners collapse thousands of users into one key, while an attacker rotates addresses freely. Key on API key or account, with IP as a secondary coarse guard.

Don't return 503 for quota exhaustion. 503 tells clients and load balancers the server is down, which triggers health-check failures and fleet-wide retries. 429 scopes the problem to one caller and keeps the retry policy sane. (→ Item 68)

Don't omit Retry-After and expect good client behaviour. Without it, naive clients retry immediately and turn your limiter into a load amplifier.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Fixed-window counting is close enough to a sliding window."

✅ Reality: It permits exactly twice the limit across a window boundary — 100 requests at 0:59.9 and 100 more at 1:00.1 is 200 in 200 ms, all allowed. If the limit protects a downstream with a hard concurrency ceiling, that 2× is the spike that breaks it.

❌ Misconception: "A 429 means the client should stop."

✅ Reality: 429 is a retryable failure with an explicit schedule attached. The correct behaviour is to wait Retry-After, then retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Treating it as terminal drops work that would have succeeded; retrying without honouring the header keeps the limiter saturated.
